title: MLB-record $4 billion sale was long time coming for aimless LA Angels
description: Arte Moreno finally sold the Angels in the midst of an MLB-worst postseason drought.
fullText:
The hatred, the criticism, the nastiness, is all over.

They can't get Arte Moreno anymore.

Moreno, who tried to sell the Los Angeles Angels four years ago but changed his mind five months later, remained patient and finally got his price to escape baseball's rat race, just ahead of baseball's anticipated Dec. 1 lockout.

He is selling the franchise for an MLB record $4 billion to sports mogul Stan Kroenke, according to a high-ranking MLB official with knowledge of the agreement. The person spoke on the condition of anonymity because the terms of the deal were not immediately public.

Moreno, 80, who purchased the Angels in 2003, just one year after they won the World Series, becoming baseball's first Latino owner with his wife, Carole, never came close to duplicating the success.

They spent money, brought in some of the biggest stars in the sport with Albert Pujols and Josh Hamilton, and had a franchise player in Mike Trout, earned five division titles in a six-year span, but haven't made the postseason since 2014.

They have the worst team in the American League (53-85), with their postseason drought extending to 12 years, and are on pace to lose 100 games for the first time in franchise history.

Now, after enduring chants of "Sell the Team," with attendance shrinking and Angels' fans turning their backs on the franchise, Moreno decided it was time to get out.

The decision stunned some of his closest friends in the industry, although one associate said he wasn't surprised at all, believing that Moreno already showed signs of losing interest.

Really, we should have all seen this coming. When Moreno fired GM Perry Minasian in June and brought in former St. Louis Cardinals baseball chief John Mozeliak, on the advice of president Molly Jolly, Mozeliak suddenly had more autonomy that existed under the last three Angels GMs.

Mozeliak was able to trade away veteran players like outfielder Jo Adell and starter Jose Soriano for prospects at the deadline, something that Moreno would have prohibited the last two decades. Mozeliak, who brought in nine prospects at the trade deadline, even was permitted to completely restructure his front office this week.

Yet, he refused to allow Minasian to even take serious offers for Shohei Ohtani three years ago at the trade deadline, wanting to re-sign him in the off-season. When Ohtani received his free-agent offers and told Moreno that he'd come back for the same 10-year, $700 million contract that he was being offered by the Los Angeles Dodgers, Toronto Blue Jays and San Francsico Giants – including $680 million in deferrals – Moreno passed without bothering to counter.

Even with the historic amount of deferred money, Moreno told his front office, "It's still $700 million."

So, the Angels received nothing in return for the biggest marketing star in baseball history, let alone the most talented since perhaps Babe Ruth, watching the Dodgers win back-to-back World Series and bring in more than $1 billion in revenue.

While the Dodgers stole the spotlight in Los Angeles, Moreno didn't blink, with their free-agent signings so pedestrian that there was not a single press conference for a free agent in Minasian's 5 ½-year tenure.

The Angels, who have hired five managers since Mike Scioscia's departure after the 2018 season, didn't even allow Minasian to offer any managerial candidate a contract longer than one year. Moreno had planned to hire Pujols, believing that he'd simply accept the $1 million personal services contract he already had with the team as part of his 10-year, $250 million deal. When Pujols asked for more as manager, including the right to hire most of his coaches, he was rejected, and the team turned to front office executive Kurt Suzuki, who accepted a one-year deal.

Moreno now walks away with at least a $3.8 billion profit, and can sit back in his Phoenix estate eating hot dogs and drinking beers watching several ballgames a day, without having to endure any more heartache.

It now is Kroenke's baby, who also owns the Rams, the Denver Nuggets of the NBA, the Colorado Avalanche of the NHL, the Colorado Rapids of MLS and the Arsenal of the Premier League.

Kroenke, who tried to buy the Dodgers a decade ago, is expected to keep the Angels in Anaheim, and expand his footprint across the Los Angeles and Orange County landscape.

"The Angels are a storied franchise anchored in a great market," Kroenke said in a statement. "We look forward to an exciting future with the Angels organization."

So do their fans, who now will start dreaming of a day that Trout returns to the postseason before his Hall of Fame career ends.

Maybe, Anaheim once again can be the "Happiest Place on Earth."

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: MLB-record $4 billion sale was long time coming for aimless LA Angels

title: Iliman Ndiaye completes Man City switch with Enzo Fernandez set to follow
description: Ndiaye seals an exit from Everton with Jack Grealish set to go the other way in a separate deal
fullText:
Iliman Ndiaye has joined Manchester City from Everton for £60m after the FA Cup winners hijacked Tottenham's attempt to sign him.

The Senegal forward said it was the "chance of a lifetime" to join City after agreeing a five-year contract at the Etihad Stadium.

Ndiaye, whose transfer fee could rise by another £5m in add-ons, took City's summer spending past £300m, with a potential £125m to follow after they agreed a deal with Chelsea for Enzo Fernandez.

The former Sheffield United player had rejected multiple offers of a new contract with Everton, who will make a big profit after signing him from Marseille for £15m two years ago.

Ndiaye believes his style of football will make him a perfect fit for City, saying: "I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this.

"City are one of the best clubs in the world and I've seen them win everything as I've grown up. To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands.

"It's not always been easy in my career, but I always had the belief that I could play for a team challenging for the biggest prizes and now I'm here. It feels so good.

"I love to play with the ball on the floor in an attacking team that wants to score as many goals as possible. That's why I know this is the perfect fit. City fans can rest assured that I will give my all to bring more success to this incredible club."

City turned to Ndiaye after having an approach for Cody Gakpo rebuffed by Liverpool and as they looked for replacements for Savinho and Omar Marmoush, who both joined Tottenham.

Welcome to City, Iliman 🩵 pic.twitter.com/u3WWUpVQOg

City director of football Hugo Viana said: "Iliman is a very talented footballer. He's had to work incredibly hard to reach this level and in my first conversation with him it was immediately obvious how grounded he is and the determination he has to be the best player he can be.

"I've no doubt City fans will get a thrill seeing him in action for us. We know this club develops players. We make a commitment to every single player we sign that we will make them better footballers.

"I am really excited to see the level Iliman can reach in the years ahead because I know for sure working with Enzo [Maresca, the manager] and his staff is going to ensure he becomes a top-class Premier League player."

Everton were trying to replace Ndiaye by signing Jack Grealish from City. They had been talking with Tottenham about separate deals in which Richarlison would return to Merseyside and Ndiaye would go to the North London club before City intervened.

In his time at Everton, Ndiaye entered their history by scoring their last ever goal at Goodison Park.

title: Printable drafting cheat sheet for 2026 PPR fantasy football leagues
description: Chet Gresham gives you his 2026 printable drafting tiers for fantasy football drafts
fullText:
Hello all! Fantasy football is back for yet another year! Can you believe it? The NFL has been given the go-ahead for another season! This plucky upstart of a league may just make it after all. And as long as the NFL is still churning out football games, I'll have my drafting tiers for all of you fake footballers. There is plenty of drafting software out there now that can help when you sit down to pick your team, but will they be FREE like my tiers? Will they! No. They probably won't.

My tiers are like other tiers you'll find out there in the wild, but these are in PDF form and are printable! This new fangled technology has disrupted the whole fantasy football market! I always draft from printed tiers because it's easier to see the whole picture of the draft with all the positions and players on one page grouped into tiers of similar value. Give it a go!

Josh Jacobs has been put on the exempt list by the league. How long he stays on it or how long a suspension might be is still unknown. We haven't heard any reports that can lead us at this point. That means we need to be careful and only draft Jacobs if he falls far enough that our team won't be hurt much if we have to drop him.

Marshawn Lloyd gets a big boost if Jacobs misses time. It is still tough to trust his health and the aforementioned unknown timeline for Jacobs. I have a feeling that someone will make the plunge for both backs earlier than I would.

Jordyn Tyson landed on the PUP list to start the season, making hi miss at least four games. This helps boost Chris Olave and Juwan Johnson, while Alvin Kamara didn't land on the PUP list, but should miss some time to start the season. That should give Travis Etienne a head start in fantasy.

First off, I really want to grab two running backs from Tier 2. If I get the first or second pick, I'll grab Jahmyr Gibbs or Bijan Robinson. That gives me tremendous fantasy floor and upside and lets me go with the best pick between a wide receiver and running back.

Secondly, I love the first three tiers of wide receivers. After I get my two running backs, I want to go hard in grabbing wide receivers from Tier 3 or Tier 2 if any have fallen.

Thirdly, tight end is deep this year and I don't feel the need to use a top pick on one of the true studs. I will most-likely grab someone from Tier 3. If I happen to miss all the TEs through Tier 3, I'll probably grab two tight ends to stream, unless I have really short benches and then I'll stream from the waiver wire.

Fourthly, I see quarterback as deep as well. Sure, I'd love Josh Allen, but I think the strategic move is to wait, especially in home leagues that often grab QBs early. Which QB I get will probably depend a lot on how the draft goes. If we get into the 6th or 7th round, and someone from Tier 2 has fallen, I'll grab him. If not, I'll feel pretty good about getting someone from Tier 4. Jaxson Dart, who is in Tier 4, has a caveat in that I want to make sure I have a usable backup for him, as he spends way too much time in the medical tent.

Fifthly, I almost always wait until the final two rounds for kicker and defense. This is tried and true and I stick by it, but, if somehow Brandon Aubrey falls far enough, and I'm in a league that only starts QB, RB, RB, WR, WR, FLEX, K, D/ST, then kicker takes up a decent portion of your total score each week. Aubrey is going to have some 20 point weeks and average in the double-digits. That can be an edge. Also, be sure to check kicker scoring. If they give you a big boost for 50 and 60 yard field goals, try to get Aubrey.

title: Surprise: Liverpool pick striker to backup Alexander Isak
description: Alexander Isak will be expected to finally get his Liverpool career off the ground this season.The Sweden international spent the vast majority of the 2026-27 campaign on the bench which is far from i...
fullText:
Alexander Isak will be expected to finally get his Liverpool career off the ground this season.

The Sweden international spent the vast majority of the 2026-27 campaign on the bench which is far from ideal for a club-record signing.

However, now that he's back fit and raring to go, Andoni Iraola will undoubtedly be looking towards the towering striker to lead his attack.

Isak has already managed to get his first Premier League goal of the season but, from the way that he's performed so far, he doesn't look like he's worth anywhere the £125 million that Liverpool spent on him.

But, with Hugo Ekitike out until at least January, Isak is going to have to step up his game or Liverpool will be forced to get creative.

Liverpool's academy is easily one of the best in the Premier League.

Legends such as Jamie Carragher, Steven Gerrard and Trent Alexander-Arnold have all made their way through the Anfield ranks and have gone on to be written in Liverpool's history books.

Indeed, some, such as Alexander-Arnold and Curtis Jones may have packed their bags and left but that doesn't mean that they're not talented.

At the moment, it feels like Liverpool have a lot of solid youngsters who are on the verge of breaking into Liverpool's first-team squad.

Lewis Koumas, Trey Nyoni and James McConnell have all been linked with having a regular role for Iraola this term.

But now, a player who fans thought would be exiting Anfield could be about to become Isak's backup.

"An update on Jayden Danns: he is going to remain at Liverpool with the aim of showing he can contribute for Andoni Iraola," Dominic King shared via X.

"It's a significant, too, as if the 134-year sequence of a local player representing the club is to continue, Danns will be the one to do it."

Liverpool's attack is one of their main areas to have had a question mark hanging over it this summer.

The transfer of Bradley Barcola was finally announced after what felt like months of negotiations and, Victor Munoz was also handed his first Premier League start for the club.

However, since some of the Reds' players are still carrying injuries from last term, some aren't available to play for Liverpool right from the start.

One of those being, Ekitike. As mentioned, the former Frankfurt man suffered a season-ending injury towards the end of last term and isn't scheduled to return until January at the earliest.

This means that, among their senior players, only Isak is a natural striker.

But, since Liverpool were undecided about what to do with Danns, they now seem to be giving him a chance to prove his worth.

Danns has had a tough time with injuries over the last couple of years but, now that he's fit and ready to play, this could be the best chance he'll ever get to prove why he deserves to be a Liverpool player.

Here's hoping he doesn't bottle it as, a homegrown striker could be exactly what the Reds need right now.

title: Monaco drop their asking price for Chelsea target Lamine Camara as Folarin Balogun’s move to Everton collapses
description: Monaco have dropped their asking price for Lamine Camara (22) to €50m plus add-ons, according to a report from Romain Molina. The Senegalese international midfielder has been the subject of interest...
fullText:
Monaco have dropped their asking price for Lamine Camara (22) to €50m plus add-ons, according to a report from Romain Molina. The Senegalese international midfielder has been the subject of interest from Chelsea on the final day of the transfer window. Negotiations between the two clubs have since collapsed due to the Principality club's asking price.

Earlier today, Monaco's sporting director Thiago Scuro was demanding that the Blues pay in the region of €70m for the 22-year-old midfielder. The Premier League were unwilling to negotiate at this price and hoping to complete a deal closer to €50m. The Ligue 1 club were not under pressure to sell the Senegalese international with Folarin Balogun agreeing to join Everton. However, the American international striker has since failed his medical and his prospective move to Merseyside appears to have collapsed.

With Balogun now staying at the Stade Louis II, Les Monégasques are under pressure to sell before the end of the window. Therefore, Molina understands they have reduced their asking price for Camara to encourage Chelsea to return to the negotiating table. It remains to be seen if the West London club will return to negotiations with just shy of two hours remaining of the summer transfer window.

title: Ex-Cowboys QB Predicted To Become “Final Nail In Shedeur Sanders’ Time With Browns”: Analyst
description: Since former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Joe Milton III is now available, the Cleveland Browns might be interested in signing him. This may not be good news for Shedeur Sanders if Browns reporter Jared Mueller is to be believed. Bringing in Milton will likely mean that either Sanders, Dillon Gabriel or the rookie, Taylen Green, will […] The post Ex-Cowboys QB Predicted To Become “Final Nail In Shedeur Sanders’ Time With Browns”: Analyst appeared first on Gridiron Heroics.
fullText:
Since former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Joe Milton III is now available, the Cleveland Browns might be interested in signing him. This may not be good news for Shedeur Sanders if Browns reporter Jared Mueller is to be believed.

Bringing in Milton will likely mean that either Sanders, Dillon Gabriel or the rookie, Taylen Green, will have to leave, because having five quarterbacks is a non-brainer. Even four quarterbacks, which the Browns currently have on their roster, is too much.

Since Milton has experience and Green is a rookie, Sanders is the most likely player to be let go if Milton is signed as per Mueller.

"Whatever you think about Sanders' talent, last year he lost a quarterback competition to the aged Joe Flacco and the undersized Gabriel," Mueller writes. "All three played poorly in 2025. Then, this year with a new coaching staff and added talent around him, Sanders lost a quarterback competition to Deshaun Watson, who hasn't been good for half a decade and is coming off missing a year and a half of football. None of that screams that the Cleveland organization is high on Sanders."

"Claiming Milton could just be the final nail in Sanders' time with the Browns," Mueller added.

If the Browns decide to replace Sanders with Milton, general manager Andrew Berry might trade Sanders to a team looking for a young QB with high potential. However, this year, even with new coaches and better teammates, Sanders lost the QB1 competition to veteran Watson.

Watson said on Monday that he did not know he would start until coach Monken told him that morning.

"This is what I've been working for for two years, to show that I'm capable of being the starter for one of the 32 organizations in this league," Watson said. "It felt good and a lot of excitement, but it comes with a lot of work, too."

Monken said that the Browns do not plan to change their starting QB from week to week.

"I think Shedeur has done a great job, come a long ways, and we're excited about his future," Monken added, "but this is not a week-to-week decision."

Instead of getting upset, Sanders took the high road and spoke out against the fans who booed Watson in the preseason game vs. the Buffalo Bills.

"I don't appreciate that at all," Sanders said. "Just, regardless of competition, we all human beings, and I think we all need to understand that."

"Just for all the fans and everything, I really appreciate ya'll showing up and everything," he added. "And however ya'll feel about the situation, about with Deshaun, about with everything, still I think it's about bigger purpose of just respect."

The Browns will play their Week 1 game on Sunday, September 13, against the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium.

title: Dodgers activate catchers Will Smith, Dalton Rushing from injured list ahead of series vs. Cardinals
description: L.A. gets a boost to begin September as its top two catchers come off the IL.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Dodgers announced Tuesday they have activated catchers Will Smith and Dalton Rushing.

Also included in the franchise's flurry of moves was activating LHP Justin Wrobleski and adding Alex Freeland to the roster. Outfielder Alek Thomas was optioned to Triple-A, and catcher Ben Rortvedt was designated for assignment.

Smith has been away from the Dodgers for nearly three months while dealing with an inflamed disk in his neck.

Before getting hurt, LA's starting catcher played in only 52 games. He was having a down year, slashing only .249/.338/.382 with six home runs and 23 RBI.

Rushing has played in 74 games this season. He was faring slightly better than Smith at the plate, slashing .253/.335/.475 with 12 home runs and 36 RBI. Rushing was sidelined after dealing with elbow soreness. After testing, it was revealed he had a slight tear in his UCL.

The catcher avoided surgery, but he is expected to be done catching for the season. As such, it remains to be seen how exactly manager Dave Roberts plans to use him, as Shohei Ohtani tends to be the team's DH and Los Angeles wouldn't want to take Ohtani's bat out of the lineup for Rushing.

The Dodgers have not been able to replicate Smith's or Rushing's production behind the plate. Los Angeles went with a combination of Hunter Feducia and Rortvedt. Feduccia was hitting .262 in 20 games, while Rortvedt played in 16 games and was hitting just .185.

Despite not having solid production from a stand-in catcher, the Dodgers still have an 82-55 record ahead of Tuesday's series opener against the St. Louis Cardinals.

Los Angeles is sitting in first place in the NL West, with a 9.5-game lead over the San Diego Padres.

title: Ndiaye: My heart was set on joining City
description: New signing Iliman Ndiaye has expressed his joy at sealing a summer transfer deadline day move to the Etihad, declaring: ‘There was nothing else I wanted other than to join Manchester City.’ Men's...
fullText:
New signing Iliman Ndiaye has expressed his joy at sealing a summer transfer deadline day move to the Etihad, declaring: 'There was nothing else I wanted other than to join Manchester City.'

The Senegalese international has become City's latest 2026 summer recruit, further bolstering Enzo Maresca's exciting new-look squad after sealing a move from Everton where he has shone bright for the past few seasons.

The 26-year-old attacking midfielder/winger has signed a five-year contract, one that will keep him at City through to the summer of 2031.

After putting pen to paper on the deal, Ndiaye revealed how immensely proud he was to have joined City.

And he revealed that after speaking with both manager Enzo Maresca and Director of Football Hugo Viana, his heart had been set on coming to the Etihad and how he was convinced he and City made for the perfect fit.

"It's easy to make the decision about whether you want to be at Manchester City or not," Ndiaye said.

"You can see the recent history; you want to be part of that project.

"They talked to me about where we could go, what we could achieve with me in the team, and I was interested from the beginning.

"There was nothing else that I wanted other than joining Manchester City.

"Obviously, you want to be part of this new project.  I've seen recently what they've been doing, and I feel like I will fit right in it.

"It's an unbelievable moment. I've worked so hard to get to this point and I'm super excited and really grateful for this opportunity."

Now that he has clinched the move up the M62, Ndiaye said his hopes and ambitions were simple and clearcut.

Namely to play his part in helping the Club go on to achieve even more silverware looking both to this season and beyond.

"Wherever you are, you want to win games and trophies," Ndiaye pointed out.

"You have your solo targets as well but most importantly; it's the team target.

"When you think about the team, if you work hard, it will come naturally.

"If you have the mindset to do it for the team and the fans, then the targets will come by itself."

title: Browns coach Todd Monken didn't watch previous Deshaun Watson tape, wants to believe all his players are 'elite'
description: Deshaun Watson has struggled since Cleveland traded for him.
fullText:
It doesn't take an advanced football mind to see that Deshaun Watson hasn't been a good starting quarterback since the Cleveland Browns acquired him.

It isn't the job of observers to fix Watson though. That is Browns head coach Todd Monken's job, especially since he named Watson his starting quarterback for the regular season.

And you'd think that the man in charge of the coaching staff that is now in charge of reviving Watson's career would watch a lot of tape to diagnose what has gone wrong since Watson joined the Browns in 2022. You'd be wrong.

Monken, who has been refreshingly honest with the media since becoming Browns coach, made a pretty startling confession on Tuesday: He has not watched any of Watson's old Browns games since becoming coach. His reasoning is very cheery, but we'll see if it works out.

Monken was asked about Watson's previous tape with the Browns, and he had a curveball for an answer.

"To be honest, haven't looked at it," Monken told the media, via Daryl Ruiter of 92.3 The Fan in Cleveland. "Only from afar. People say, 'Well you had to have looked at it.' Well, not really."

Monken said he looked at it when he was "down the road," presumably meaning when he was Baltimore Ravens' offensive coordinator from 2023-25. That's not the same as watching it to diagnose issues with a player you'll be working closely with.

Why hasn't he watched it? Monken explained that he wants to come in believe all his new players are elite.

"I try to take everything at face value. What I see," Monken said. "I think we owe that to our players.

"I want to go into it thinking every player we have is elite, and all they have to do is prove me right."

Good news: Todd Monken hasn’t watched Deshaun Watson’s tape from the 19 games he’s played for #Browns. 

Bad news: Todd Monken hasn’t watched Deshaun Watson’s tape from the 19 games he’s played for #Browns. pic.twitter.com/jryMwyPp3P

Monken continued by saying the previous games were with "different staff, different system," and that's fair. Watson will be asked to do different things than he had been doing.

But blindly believing Watson is elite and hoping he'll prove the coaches right is an curious approach.

Watson should be thankful Monken didn't watch the tape of his 19 Browns starts. He wouldn't have found many positives.

Watson has been bad for the Browns. But his glory days with the Texans (and, likely more important, his massive uncuttable contract) preceded him. Watson seemed to be anointed as the starter before Monken ever was hired, and it played out that way: Watson was the QB1 through most of the offseason and named the Week 1 starter even when Shedeur Sanders thoroughly outplayed him in the second preseason game before the announcement.

Perhaps it would be prudent to watch Watson's his glory days at Clemson and then in Houston, and spot what has gone so wrong in Cleveland. It's rare for a quarterback to completely fall off at a prime age the way Watson has. But Monken obviously is taking a different approach.

A clean slate might be what Watson needs, though that will be extremely difficult to find in Cleveland, especially after Watson ripped Browns fans. But we'll get to see starting in Week 1 if he turns it around. Monken won't be able to avoid watching the tape of those games. We'll find out if he likes what he sees.

title: Why Government Bond Yields Are Rising and Causing Alarm
description: Government borrowing costs have been surging around the world as investors demand more compensation to entice them to hold longer-maturity debt. Yields on 30-year Japanese government bonds are near all-time highs at 4.19%, while 30-year UK government bond yields are at their highest since 1998. A Bloomberg gauge tracking government debt across the Group of Seven countries now yields its highest on average since September 2000.
fullText: MarketsExplainerBy George Nixon, Ye Xie, and Greg RitchieSaveGovernment borrowing costs have been surging around the world as investors demand more compensation to entice them to hold longer-maturity debt. Yields on 30-year Japanese government bonds are near all-time highs at 4.19%, while 30-year UK government bond yields are at their highest since 1998. A Bloomberg gauge tracking government debt across the Group of Seven countries now yields its highest on average since September 2000.Investors’ retreat from long-dated sovereign debt has been driven by a range of concerns, including mounting fiscal deficits and stubborn inflation. Governments are also having to compete for investor attention as technology companies issue massive amounts of debt to fund the buildout of artificial-intelligence infrastructure.

title: Bond Traders Snap Up Protection Against Soaring Treasury Yields
description: Traders are scrambling to shield their portfolios against further losses in Treasuries, as worries over the budget deficit and inflation push yields toward multiyear highs.
fullText: MarketsBy Edward Bolingbroke and Greg RitchieSaveTraders are scrambling to shield their portfolios against further losses in Treasuries, as worries over the budget deficit and inflation push yields toward multiyear highs.Investors have shelled out millions of dollars over recent sessions on Treasury options that would benefit if yields continued climbing. Standouts include a Monday trade that took a $6.5 million position targeting the 30-year yield rising to as high as 5.7% by the end of November. title: Claude Code setup I built for a bike workshop's 20-year-old classic ASP system
description: Five months of Claude Code building its own tooling, steered by me, across a fleet of machines and a handful of separate codebases — a proper todo database, two-tier memory, and a session routine that runs itself.
fullText:
Five months of Claude Code building its own tooling, steered by me, across a fleet of machines and a handful of separate codebases — a proper todo database, two-tier memory, and a session routine that runs itself.

Most write-ups of AI coding assistants are about a clever prompt or a plugin you can install. This one's about something slower, and I think more useful: having the assistant build its own tooling over months, in a git repo, tuned to exactly how you work.

I've been running Claude Code across a real business for the past five months. Not one codebase but a small portfolio: the oldest and gnarliest is a bike workshop's booking system — twenty years of classic ASP I wrote myself, on Windows, inevitably — and around it a separate public website, a stack of Node services that didn't exist before, a second business's system, and the assistant's own tooling. Each its own git repo, all run from the same machines: Proxmox hosts, Linux servers, a few laptops, a work desktop, and an Android phone running Claude Code in a terminal. Before Claude Code, the oldest of these had been quietly stagnating. Five months on it's been optimised, bug-fixed, and given features that had sat on the someday list for years, while the newer projects grew up beside it. Claude Code itself grew the same way — one small script at a time — into something that knows my machines, remembers its own mistakes, tracks its own work, and starts and ends every session with a single word.

None of that was planned. There's a stripped-down, sanitised example on GitHub — the bootstrap script, the memory layout, the todo CLI, the session hooks:

▸ Demo repo: github.com/pyfd/self-improving-claude-code

Everything below is real and in daily use. Take the ideas, not the specifics — the specifics are shaped like my life, which is rather the point.

Everything lives in one git repo of dotfiles and scripts. Every machine clones it and runs a single bootstrap: SSH config, shell aliases, git hooks, Claude Code settings, and Claude's memory. Bare to working in about ten minutes, and every machine behaves the same.

The other half of the glue is Tailscale: every machine sits on the same tailnet, so the phone in a café reaches the same todo database and dashboards as the laptop at home.

git moves the tooling; Tailscale moves the traffic.

Together they're the foundation. Claude's whole configuration is versioned, synced and reviewable. Improve the tooling on one machine and every machine has it at the next pull — and once the config is just a repo, the assistant can improve itself the same way it improves your code.

Most AI task setups are a markdown file the model edits. Fine for one person on one machine; it falls apart the moment two sessions run at once, or you jot a task on your phone that the laptop needs to see.

Ours is a SQLite database on a server, behind a small authenticated API, with an append-only event log — every add, close, edit and note records who, when and why. On top of that:

Task state is shared, audited infrastructure — not a file the model politely edits.

Claude Code loads instruction files into every session, and context is a budget. The obvious approach — one ever-growing "remember this" file — quietly fails: it bloats until parts of it stop loading.

So, two tiers. The first is always loaded: the global instructions plus a memory index — one line per memory, a title and a one-sentence hook. A hundred-odd lines, pruned hard, because every line is paid for on every session. The second tier is a folder of individual memory files — preferences, project state, runbooks, and a lot of hard-won corrections ("never rsync --delete to a server" — earned the day a stray --delete wiped nineteen files). A file is read only when its topic comes up.

The index is the bridge: it tells each session what detail exists and when to fetch it. Hot and cold storage. The discipline is all in the curation — a vague line never gets fetched, too many lines blows the budget, and past a hard ceiling the index drops its own tail with no warning. It just quietly forgets.

The memory folder lives in the dotfiles repo, so memories sync across the fleet like everything else: something learned on the phone is known to the laptop by the next pull.

The most valuable memory isn't a set of best practices — it's a written record of every mistake the assistant has made for me, and why. You can't download that.

Sessions have a shape, so we made the shape executable.

Typing go pulls the dotfiles, re-runs the bootstrap and syncs every project repo — flushing the offline todo queue, regenerating the mirrors, and checking the servers for uncommitted drift on the way. One word, and the session starts from a known-good state, whichever machine I'm on.

fin is the complement, not the reverse: go restores a known-good state, fin captures what changed. It updates every doc whose subject moved — changelog, project state, any spec the work touched — reconciles the todo flags, writes a resume point (a machine-stamped note saying exactly where to pick up), closes finished todos with the commit hash as the reason, then commits, pushes and syncs out.

Most of what I've described, Claude built. Because the whole configuration is just a repo, it edits its own tooling the way it edits any of the projects — a branch, a diff, a commit you can read afterwards.

That only works because the self-modification runs through the same discipline as everything else. Every change lands with a changelog entry; every closed todo records why; every memory carries the reason it exists. When the assistant gets something wrong, the fix isn't a scolding that evaporates when the chat ends — it's a new memory or guard rail, written down so the next session can't repeat it.

None of it was designed up front. The todo database exists because two sessions once clobbered the markdown file it replaced. The deploy guards exist because a deploy once went out wrong. The curation rules exist because the index blew its budget and forgot its own tail. It accreted, one correction at a time.

The corrections stuck because they live in the repo, not in my head.

None of this would matter if it were toys. The same system runs actual operations: an alerting stack Claude built and maintains, dashboards for everything (including its own token usage, per machine and per model), and guard rails written after its own mistakes — a pre-commit hook that refuses a commit until the changelog is staged (it blocked me twice while I assembled the example repo for this article — precisely its job), and a deploy that won't touch the live site until the dev version's been eyeballed in a real browser. It holds itself to rules it learned the hard way.

While I was building this, a genre of article appeared — "I cancelled $220 of monthly subscriptions, five Claude Code plugins replaced them all." They're not wrong, and if you're paying separately for a security scanner, a PR-review bot and a browser-testing service, read one.

Still: should I have just installed the plugins instead? I evaluated the popular ones, and out of it fell a small lens I now use before adding anything — plugin, MCP server, framework:

Plugins are priced in dollars. The real currency is RAM.

Against those five, the famous plugins mostly came out "already covered" — not because they're bad, but because five months of tooling tuned to your exact setup is a high bar. It should be; that's the point of building rather than installing.

If you're starting fresh, install the plugins. Building it yourself only wins when three things are true: you'll use the system daily for years, so the tuning compounds; your environment is genuinely odd (a fleet, a phone, a legacy stack, a real business's guard rails); and you're willing to let the assistant maintain its own tooling, with the discipline that stops that becoming chaos.

If that's you, start small. One repo. One bootstrap script. A memory index you actually prune. The rest builds up on its own — the demo repo above is roughly where I was after the first fortnight.

The interesting outcome isn't saving a subscription. It's a tool that knows how you work, on every machine you own, with a written record of every mistake it's ever made for you. That doesn't come from a directory. It builds up, in a git repo, a little at a time.

Two pieces wouldn't fit here and deserve write-ups of their own:

Happy to talk any of it through — comments are open below, or over on the demo repo.

Written with, inevitably, Claude Code.

title: Dev-sandbox – One bash script to isolate AI coding agents with Podman
description: Run untrusted code and AI agents in isolated Podman containers with krun microVMs.  Network control, SSH, Privoxy proxy — one self-contained bash script. - kosmrljt/dev-sandbox
fullText:
Run AI coding agents in isolated Podman containers, optionally with krun microVMs.

For Linux distributions with Podman support. Developed and tested on Fedora 44.

One self-contained bash script. No dependencies beyond Podman. Configure profiles, build, run — everything in a single file.

AI coding agents need shell access and run arbitrary code. Without isolation:

dev-sandbox runs each agent in its own isolated environment with only the current project directory visible.

What this does not prevent: an agent can write to .git/hooks and persistent volumes, which execute on the next run. See docs/SECURITY.md.

The first run builds images (~1.6 GB, several minutes). Subsequent runs start in seconds. The default profile is configured for Claude Code — edit the script to change.

Once inside, you are in an isolated container:

Four built-in profiles with color-coded prompts. Each is isolated — separate volumes, credentials, and settings.

Show resolved settings for any profile:

krun runs its own Linux kernel inside a microVM — a different isolation boundary than container namespaces. Standard container shares the host kernel but has full support for SSH tunneling and firewall.

Default is krun. Architecture details: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

Defaults apply to all profiles. Each profile only overrides what differs:

Settings resolve: CLI flag > Profile > Environment > Default.

Full configuration reference: docs/CONFIGURATION.md.

Optional: gocryptfs for encrypted directories, btrfs for quotas and snapshots.

urllight — SOCKS5 proxy with live terminal dashboard. Route sandbox traffic through it to see every connection and DNS query.

Inspired by the Fedora Magazine article on sandboxing AI agents with microVMs. Built through iterative pair programming with Claude (Anthropic).

title: New system views in PostgreSQL 19
description: PostgreSQL 19 adds four system views that make lock contention, recovery state, autovacuum priorities, and dynamic shared memory allocations easier to inspect.
fullText:
While writing about the monitoring improvements in PostgreSQL 19 and preparing my new talk on Postgres observability for PostgreSQL Conference Europe in October, I noticed the system views got their own section in this release. The last time they were similarly highlighted was in PG13 and PG14. So I decided the system views need a blog of their own to go through what has changed. PostgreSQL 19 adds four new views, pg_stat_lock, pg_stat_recovery, pg_stat_autovacuum_scores, and pg_dsm_registry_allocations, each deserving more than the one-line mention they got in my monitoring blog, so here is the tour.

Disclaimer: PostgreSQL 19 is still in beta as I write this and this area has already seen columns renamed mid-cycle; things can still change or get reverted before GA. The release notes will be the final word.

Locks are a special interest of mine 😀 Last year, I spoke at 16 conferences with a talk called "Anatomy of Table-Level Locks in PostgreSQL". If you're interested, some of those talks were recorded and are available on YouTube. So, you can imagine how excited I was to see a new locks view in PostgreSQL 19.

Until now your options for understanding lock contention were pg_locks (a snapshot of right now, no history) and log_lock_waits output (history, but you have to parse logs to aggregate the logs yourself, though PostgreSQL 19 now turns it on by default, a change I covered in my monitoring post).

PostgreSQL 19 adds pg_stat_lock (a patch by Bertrand Drouvot §): cumulative, cluster-wide lock statistics with one row per lock type (locktype). The name locktype might be a little confusing. It is not the lock mode (such as ACCESS EXCLUSIVE or ROW SHARE) but the kind of lockable object (showing what was being locked) and there are 12 of them: relation, transactionid, tuple, extend, page, object, advisory, virtualxid, spectoken, applytransaction, frozenid, userlock.

The view itself is a thin wrapper around the new function pg_stat_get_lock().

The newly introduced pg_stat_get_lock() function does not have a docs page, since like most of the pg_stat_get_* functions, it only exists to back the view, but it's there if you want to query it directly.

One important detail: waits and wait_time only count locks that were successfully acquired after waiting longer than deadlock_timeout (1 second by default), so pg_stat_lock isn't a counter of every lock wait.

Let's run some queries, I have two psql sessions to demo the lock contention. The first session takes a lock on the demo table and holds it by keeping the transaction open:

The second session tries to lock the same table and cannot acquire the lock (until session 1 commits):

After the 2.5 seconds, session 1 commits and session 2 finally gets its lock. Since that wait lasted longer than the default deadlock_timeout of 1s and ended in a successful acquisition, it gets counted. To see that, let’s query the view:

Before starting the demo, I reset the lock statistics with pg_stat_reset_shared('lock'), so the numbers below come from only this scenario.

pg_stat_reset_shared() resets cluster-wide statistics for a given target, such as 'wal', 'io' or 'bgwriter'. The 'lock' target is new in PostgreSQL 19, added together with the pg_stat_lock view.

This result shows that session 2 had to wait 2.2 seconds (out of 2.5 second session 1 hoarded the table) to acquire the lock. The 0.3 second difference reflects session 2 asking for the lock, a moment after session 1 took it.

On a real system, we won’t be chasing a single wait, so we’ll have to query lock types together with waits:

pg_stat_lock view always returns all 12 lock types, WHERE waits > 0 filters out those without recorded contention. We then order by total wait time and calculate the average wait per lock type. A high total wait time can point to a frequently contended lock type, while a high average can reveal fewer but longer stalls.

I thought the fastpath_exceeded counter in the pg_stat_lock view was worth digging into, so I gave it its own section 🙂 For speed, each backend keeps a small set of fast-path slots for the most common locks that rarely conflict with anything. When a query needs more locks than the slot can hold, the extras fall back to the slower shared lock table and this counter ticks (every time, no deadlock_timeout threshold here).

fastpath_exceeded can be particularly interesting for partition-heavy workloads, where a single query may need to lock many relations.

If the fastpath_exceeded counter grows on your partition-heavy workload, that's a direct hint to raise max_locks_per_transaction. Starting from PostgreSQL 18, the fast-path slot count derives from it (before that it was fixed at 16; Christophe Pettus has an excellent write-up of that era). PostgreSQL 19 doubled the default max_locks_per_transaction from 64 to 128 (Heikki Linnakangas §).

To make the demo easy, let's create a partitioned table with more partitions than the fast-path slots can cover. I chose 140 partitions, more than the new default 128. (Postgres's own regression test uses the same trick, creating max_locks_per_transaction + 10 partitions.)

Then reset the counters again for a clean read, and scan the table once; a plain SELECT count(*) has to lock the parent and every partition:

The count exceeds 140 because Postgres counts every over-limit lock acquisition attempt, and partitions can be locked during both planning and execution. The exact number may vary between runs; what matters is that it is non-zero, this workload spills out of the fast path.

If you have ever built a standby health check, you have probably used some or all of these functions to check the standby state: pg_is_in_recovery(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(), pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp(), pg_get_wal_replay_pause_state(). Each of these functions reads the shared recovery state under its own lock, at a slightly different moment. Even if you wrap them in a single view, which is what we DBAs used to do, the values are not guaranteed to be consistent with each other because replay keeps advancing between the calls.

pg_stat_recovery (Xuneng Zhou §, with a fix by Shinya Kato §) assembles all this information in one row, read as a single atomic snapshot, so all fields are consistent with each other.

The pg_stat_recovery view also exposes information that previously had no SQL interface: the start LSN of the last replayed record, the replay timelines, the end position of the record currently being replayed, and whether a promotion has been triggered. Previously, SQL could only tell you when a promotion had completed through pg_is_in_recovery() returning false, not that one was already underway.

If you maintain HA tooling, this is a good time to update it. If you run health checks every few seconds, getting a consistent view of the recovery state with one query instead of several is a small but nice win.

I will cover two changes in this section: a new autovacuum behaviour and a view (pg_stat_autovacuum_scores) to watch it.

First, the behavior. PostgreSQL 19 changes how autovacuum decides what to work on first. Before PostgreSQL 19, autovacuum processed tables in the order it found them in pg_class. Now, each worker calculates a score for every table based on how close it is to (or how far past) its autovacuum thresholds: XID age, multixact age, dead tuples, inserts and analyze staleness. The highest score wins, so tables needing attention most are processed first.

Five new autovacuum_*_score_weight parameters (all defaulting to 1.0) let you set weights for the components. Setting all of them to 0.0 restores the pre-19 ordering. Nathan Bossart’s commit calls this "a baby step towards smarter autovacuum workers".

The second change surfaces these stats: pg_stat_autovacuum_scores (Sami Imseih §) exposes these scores per table (including TOAST tables and system catalogs) in the current database, revealing what tables autovacuum prioritizes.

Table 3: pg_stat_autovacuum_scores view

Let’s run a few queries to see it working. I created a 1000 row table, analyzed it and deleted 400 rows:

Then asked the pg_stat_autovacuum_scores view what autovacuum thinks of my tables:

Where does 2.67 come from? Autovacuum decides when to act using thresholds computed from the table's row count. For analyze, the default is 50 + 0.1 × rows → for our 1000 row table, that's 150. We changed 400 rows, so the analyze score is 400 / 150 = 2.67.

The deletes crossed the vacuum threshold too: 50 + 0.2 × 1000 = 250, giving 400 / 250 = 1.60. Since the overall score is the highest component, av_demo gets 2.67 and qualifies for both vacuum and analyze.

for_wraparound derives from a different calculation entirely, not row changes, but age. As in, how far the table's oldest unfrozen transaction ID has drifted toward autovacuum_freeze_max_age (200 million transactions by default). Our freshly created table is nowhere near that threshold, so it is false.

pg_stat_autovacuum_scores computes scores from current statistics while autovacuum workers score the tables whenever they wake up. The two moments can differ, so treat the view as a strong hint of what autovacuum will prioritize, not a guarantee.

A smaller one: extensions increasingly allocate shared memory through the DSM registry, which spares them from needing shared_preload_libraries (and a restart) just to get shared memory. Until now that memory wasn't visible from SQL.

DSM stands for dynamic shared memory: shared memory created at runtime, unlike the main shared memory area, which is allocated once at server start (which is why extensions needing shared state traditionally required shared_preload_libraries and a restart). The DSM registry, added in PostgreSQL 17 (Nathan Bossart §), lets backends create, find and attach to these shared memory segments by name. This means extensions get shared state with a plain CREATE EXTENSION, no restart. 

This new pg_dsm_registry_allocations view (Florents Tselai §, extended by Nathan Bossart §) lists each registry entry with its name, type (segment, area or hash) and size. A NULL size means the entry failed to initialize.

Table 4: pg_dsm_registry_allocations view

Thanks for reading this far! I hope the new system views excite you as much as they do me. We’re all counting down the days to PostgreSQL 19 and I’m already wishing everyone happy upgrades!

I will be talking about PostgreSQL 19 observability at PostgreSQL Conference Europe in October, and several of the topics I covered here will make an appearance. Come say hi if you plan to be in Valencia! 👋

title: Five Sleep-Tracking Hacks Every Garmin User Should Know
description: If you're going to train hard, you need to know how to recover hard, too.
fullText:
Garmin isn't the first name people tend to bring up when they talk about sleep tracking wearables—Whoop or Oura has that market cornered. But if you already live in the Garmin ecosystem, you don't need to buy a second device just to get better sleep insights. You can use the device you have— you mostly only need to know where to look and how to set it up. Here are five ways to get more out of the sleep tracking tools you already have.

Start by customizing your Garmin to focus on sleep insights. On your watch, press and hold the menu button, go into Settings, then Glances, and drag your Sleep glance up near the top, so it's one of the first things you see when you wake up and check your wrist.

While you're in there, turn on Sleep Coach if it isn't already enabled. It lives under Settings > Sleep, and once it's on, it compares your recent sleep history against your training load and tells you roughly how much sleep you need that specific night, not just a flat eight-hour target.

It's also worth understanding what's actually happening behind your nightly sleep score, since that will explain why the number sometimes seems disconnected from how you actually feel. Garmin calculates its score from a blend of data: how long you slept, how well you slept, and what it describes as evidence of recovery activity occurring in your autonomic nervous system, derived from heart rate variability data. In plain terms, the watch is theoretically tracking the tiny changes in time between each heartbeat while you sleep, and factoring that into your score. The idea is that this can catch tough nights where your body never fully powered down, even if you were technically lying still the entire time.

Body Battery gets a lot of attention because it's a visually satisfying, supposedly simple recovery number. But it's a blended, somewhat opaque metric, and leaning on it too heavily for sleep insight can be misleading. A few numbers underneath it tell you more. When you're building your sleep dashboard I explain above, consider bringing these metrics to the top.

HRV is the most useful metric to consider. A lower-than-normal overnight HRV is one of the more reliable early signals that you're either under-recovered, coming down with something, or dealing with elevated stress your body hasn't shaken off, even on a night where you technically got enough hours.

Pulse ox and respiration rate are worth watching too, particularly together. A rising resting respiration rate or dips in blood oxygen overnight can point to disrupted breathing, poor air quality in your room, or sleeping at altitude, none of which will necessarily tank your "sleep score" but all of which affect how rested you actually feel.

And when it comes to sleep structure, pay more attention to total time in bed and how consolidated it was, versus the so-called sleep stage breakdown. Wrist-based sleep stage detection, whether on a Garmin or basically any other wrist wearable, is an estimate built from movement and heart rate patterns—not exactly clinical-grade brainwave data. No wearable is going to be completely accurate when it comes to sleep stages, so don’t read too much into those estimates. Total sleep duration (and how fragmented it was) is a sturdier number to trust.

If you ask me, naps are one of the more overlooked features in Garmin Connect. If you take a nap of 20 minutes or longer, the watch can log it as a nap rather than just idle time, which matters because it recalculates your nightly sleep requirement afterward. On most watches, you can start this manually from the activity or glance menu by selecting Nap or Rest, or the watch will detect longer stationary rest periods on its own depending on your model.

The main reason this matters: if you skip logging a nap, Garmin still assumes you need a full night's worth of recovery sleep, when you might've already banked some of it. Logging naps keeps Sleep Coach's recommendations as accurate as they can be, and can help explain why your nightly numbers might feel off.

A watch buzzing or lighting up on your wrist at 2 a.m. does nothing good for your HRV. Go into Settings > Display and turn on Sleep Mode (sometimes labeled Do Not Disturb) so the screen dims or stays off overnight, and pair it with scheduled Do Not Disturb hours under Settings > Notifications so calls, texts, and app alerts stop reaching your wrist during your sleep window.

Some Garmin models also let you set Do Not Disturb to activate automatically based on your sleep schedule, which is worth turning on so you don't have to remember it every night. Beyond just being annoying, a bright screen or a buzz against your skin can be enough to trigger a brief arousal that shows up as fragmented sleep in your data, even if you don't consciously remember waking up.

Under the Sleep section in Garmin Connect, you can log lifestyle factors like alcohol, caffeine, and other habits alongside your nightly sleep data. The value here isn't in staring at every daily fluctuation, but in spotting patterns. If you notice your deep sleep consistently drops on nights you log a drink, that's actionable information to improve your sleep hygiene. Compare that to someone who checks their HRV trend every morning with no real reference point for what's driving the ups and downs, and you realize that Lifestyle Logging is where your true insights are hiding.

For most people, the simplest version of this process is enough: just track total sleep time, your overall sleep score, and how many drinks or late caffeine you had that day. I also recommend leaving notes for yourself about whether you felt lethargic during the day, as those insights can be valuable when pattern spotting as well.

The five hacks above only work if you're wearing your watch in the right position. Wear it too loose, and it won't pick up accurate data; too tight, and it could get uncomfortable enough that you'll either take it off in your sleep or toss and turn more than you normally would.

The general rule is to wear your watch snug enough that it doesn't rotate but not so tight it leaves a mark. Optical heart rate sensors read best when they're in consistent contact with skin, so a slightly firmer fit at night than during a daytime workout is usually the right call.

If you find that wearing a watch to bed is uncomfortable no matter how you adjust it, or if sleep tracking within the Garmin ecosystem is genuinely a priority for you, it might indeed be worth leveling up to a dedicated device instead of fighting with your watch every night. Garmin's Index Sleep Monitor is a lightweight armband built specifically for overnight wear, tracking sleep stages, HRV, breathing variations, and skin temperature without the bulk of a watch on your wrist. Garmin's newer Cirqa smart band is a screen-free option that can be worn around the clock, syncing all its data back into Garmin Connect alongside anything your watch tracks during the day. Neither of these devices is a requirement for sleep tracking, but if the numbers matter to you and your watch keeps waking you up or falling off your wrist, one of these purpose-built options will get you more reliable data with a lot less friction. For more, check out Lifehacker's list of the best fitness trackers for sleep and recovery.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Reacher' You Should Watch Next
description: More binge-worthy, often book-based crime dramas about heroic loners.
fullText:
After a couple of middling movies, Reacher, the series based on a series of more than 30 novels by Lee Childs, has been a breakout hit for Prime Video. It has been renewed through at least a fifth season, and there's a spin-off on the way—Neagley, starring Maria Sten. It's not hard to understand why audiences have connected to the story of an alarmingly large man who travels from town to town getting himself into trouble while helping others out of scrapes: The plotting is fun, the show doesn't take itself too seriously, and Alan Ritchson is a great physical match for the character while also selling the drifter-with-a-heart-of-gold vibe.

If you've finished your season four binge and need something new to watch, try one of the series below. Not all of them focus on outright loners like Reacher, and none of them are quite so large, but they all are more than capable of getting the job done solo.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings. Until...it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed and, unbeknownst to her, were also government operatives. Rescuing Rose puts Peter deep inside a web of conspiracy and official corruption. (This is why I never answer the phone.) Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There are like three dozen Alex Cross books (and counting), so there's plenty of material for this ongoing series (previously adapted into a series of films back in the '90s starring Morgan Freeman). Here, the D.C.-based homicide detective and forensic psychologist is played by Aldis Hodge as a guy every bit as committed to justice as Reacher. What sets Cross apart is the fact that he's also deeply committed to his family, which, rather than adding a charming bit of domesticity to the show, only ups the stakes as Cross's investigations frequently threaten to involve his kids. Stream Cross on Prime Video and Paramount+.

Tom Clancy's signature hero has been the star of books and films (starting with The Hunt for Red October) and has, at this point, outlived his creator by over a decade—despite the fact that he is never not in mortal danger. The latest incarnation, Prime Video's streaming series, stars John Krasinski as America's favorite CIA analyst, pulled from his desk job into the field after he discovers a pattern of suspicious bank transfers involving Islamic extremists. The show has ended, but the rather awkwardly titled Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan: Ghost War movie continues the series. Stream Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan on Prime Video.

The Queen Latifah-led Equalizer reboots the 1980s series (and sidesteps the Denzel Washington movies) by spinning the premise in a slightly different direction: Latifah plays single mom Robyn McCall, an impossibly skilled former CIA operative who puts her talents to work for those in need. It splits the difference between crime and spy drama, with some episodes involving close-to-home cases and others dealing with international espionage. While the original's vibe was more about the cops being handcuffed by things like "rules" and "giving perps their basic human dignity," this one is more about those who've been failed by systems that don't care about them—and who might benefit from the help of a woman who can beat just about anyone's ass. Stream The Equalizer on Paramount+ and Tubi.

Based on a popular novel series from Joe R. Lansdale, perhaps best known for his horror and western (and horror western) books, the show rather deftly blends genres—it's a heist show, a crime drama, and a buddy comedy set in the swamps around Baton Rouge in the 1980s. James Purefoy is Hap, a blue-collar ex-con (for avoiding the Vietnam draft) trying to live a quiet life, while the late Michael Kenneth Williams is Leonard, an openly gay vet with major anger management problems. One day, Hap's ex-wife shows up with an offer: the proceeds of a bank heist were lost, and if the two help her retrieve it, they'll get a cut, while she'll use the rest of money to fund her underground leftist group. Naturally, things get complicated rather quickly. Stream Hap and Leonard on AMC+.

Coming, as it does, from John le Carré, the wellspring of many modern spy sagas, it's probably no surprise that The Night Manager (from a 1993 novel, and not to be confused with The Night Agent up above) was successful—though it certainly doesn't hurt to have a cast led by Tom Hiddleston, Hugh Laurie, and Olivia Colman. Hiddleston is Jonathan Pine, working the night shift at a luxury hotel in Switzerland when he encounters an unexpected guest: arms dealer Richard Roper (Laurie). Former Army veteran Pine had previous dealings with Roper in Cairo, and the reluctant night manager is persuaded by Foreign Office head Angela Burr (Colman) to infiltrate the criminal's organization. Though he's been recruited by British intelligence, he remains an outsider, and perpetually on his own. The second season took about ten years to come about, but a third (and final?) should arrive a bit sooner. Stream The Night Manager on Prime Video.

Bosch is a more traditional crime drama, though one that wears its neo-noir aspirations on its sleeve. Titus Welliver is in the title role as LAPD detective Harry Bosch (star of the Michael Connelly novels), kicking off the series on trial for shooting a suspect in self-defense while investigating the murder of a 12-year-old. Like Reacher, Bosch draws on skills honed in the military and pursues criminals well beyond the limits, which is not always a great thing. Stream Bosch on Prime Video.

A usually engaging combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda. A man recently released from prison takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed. It's all part of a complicated plan to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail. The new sheriff dispenses brutal justice without ever giving up his criminal ways, making him one of the greyest of TV's morally grey law-types. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

Where Reacher is a loner from the jump, Luther's arc is one of one of increasing isolation, even as he cultivates an unsavory but steadfast ally. Idris Elba is DCI John Luther—a crime-solving genius whose preexisting inner demons are enabled by his work in investigating some of the darkest and most brutal crimes. Early on, he's unable to bring murderer Alice Morgan (Ruth Wilson) to justice, and the two become entangled in ways that benefit Luther's investigations while also threatening to bring him down entirely. The series proper is concluded, but there's a second spin-off film on the way, following The Fallen Sun. Stream Luther on Hulu.

Another hero of a long-running book series (this one from Jeffery Deaver), the tracker in question is Colter Shaw (Justin Hartley), a survivalist who travels the country (in his RV, naturally) selling his skills in finding missing persons. He's joined, remotely, by a team that includes a lawyer, handler, and the requisite computer guy—but they're all just the support team. At the end of the day, Shaw's the one who's gonna find your lost uncle. Stream Tracker on Paramount+.

Man Utd fail in bid to sign Leicester midfielder Page
description: Manchester United have failed in an attempt to sign Leicester midfielder Louis Page, while Joshua Zirkzee and Harry Amass are set to stay at Old Trafford
fullText:
Manchester United have failed in their attempts to sign highly-rated midfielder Louis Page from Leicester City.

United's interest in Page was first reported by BBC Sport in August.

However, the first sign of a problem was Page being named in Leicester's starting line-up for their League One fixture against Plymouth on Tuesday.

It was then confirmed by sources the deal will not be concluded and Page will remain a Leicester player.

It is understood the Foxes wanted well in excess of £10m for the 18-year-old, who only made his first team debut in August 2025, but has already carved out an impressive reputation, making 25 appearances in total.

It was anticipated United were willing to loan Page straight back to Leicester, given they have already spent in excess of £150m on international midfielders this summer.

Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos have already made their debut, while Carlos Baleba - a £70m purchase from Brighton - will miss the next couple of weeks with a minor ankle issue.

While it transpires Page will not be arriving, it also seems certain 19-year-old full-back Harry Amass will not be leaving.

Amass spent most of pre-season as back-up left-back to Luke Shaw.

However, he has not been chosen in Michael Carrick's squad for either Premier League game so far and it was expected he would take up one of the numerous offers to sign him on loan.

But United's failure to sign an experienced left-back means Amass is set to stay, even though he will probably be Carrick's third choice given Noussair Mazraoui replaced Shaw during Sunday's 5-2 win against Ipswich.

The chances of the Old Trafford outfit signing a left-back were hampered by Joshua Zirkzee's failure to find a new club.

After talks with one Serie A outfit, Fiorentina, failed to reach a successful conclusion over the weekend, Zirkzee's hopes of being signed by Juventus were dashed when they opted to bring in Newcastle's Nick Woltemade on loan instead.

description: Vivianne Miedema will miss the start of the Women's Super League season because of a knee injury.
fullText:
Manchester City striker Vivianne Miedema will miss the beginning of the Women's Super League season with a knee injury.

It is understood that Netherlands international Miedema, 30, has not suffered an anterior cruciate ligament injury.

The club said the latest issue is also "separate to the previous knee injuries she's experienced".

Miedema scored 10 times and assisted five 

She had a largely injury-free campaign last year, although she underwent knee surgery at the end of the season.

title: Two-time Gold Cup winner Galopin Des Champs dies days after retiring
description: Two-time Cheltenham Gold Cup winner Galopin Des Champs dies aged 10, less than a week after retiring.
fullText:
Galopin Des Champs, the two-time Cheltenham Gold Cup winner, has died less than a week after being retired.

In a statement to RacingTV on Tuesday, the former jockey Ruby Walsh, said: "Sadly Galopin Des Champs suffered an injury in his field this morning and could not be saved."

Galopin Des Champs also won three Irish Gold Cups, two Savills Chases and a Punchestown Gold Cup.

The 10-year-old was retired from racing by trainer Willie Mullins last week.

When announcing his retirement, Mullins said it was because "he could not do himself justice at the level he was used to".

The jumper won the Cheltenham Gold Cup in 2023 and 2024 and won 12 races at Grade One level.

Walsh added: "He was checked a few times throughout the morning, but late in the morning when I went to get him for exercise I found him with a severe injury, high up on his near front leg. He was attended to by our vets immediately, but X-rays revealed extensive unrepairable damage.

"He was a fabulous racehorse whose short time with us has left lots of broken hearts but none more so than those of Greg, Audrey and Sarah Turley, and Adam Connolly, who looked after him for so long. He will be sadly missed."

title: Celtic sign Parma's Sorensen, with more to come before deadline
description: Celtic sign Parma midfielder Oliver Sorensen on loan shortly after assistant manager Shaun Maloney suggests the Scottish champions were working on up to four additions before finalising their Europa League squad on Wednesday.
fullText:
Celtic have completed the signing of Parma midfielder Oliver Sorensen on loan shortly after assistant manager Shaun Maloney suggested the Scottish champions were working on up to four additions before finalising their Europa League squad on Wednesday.

Sorensen will spend the season in Glasgow, with Celtic having an option to buy the 24-year-old who signed for the Italian side in August 2025 after five years with Midtjylland in Denmark.

Celtic have signed four first-team players so far this window and have also been linked with Wolverhampton Wanderers goalkeeper Sam Johnstone and PSV Eindhoven midfielder Joel van den Berg.

Maloney hopes another left-back can be recruited to compete with Scotland international Kieran Tierney, while "it's possible" Japan midfielder Reo Hatate could move on and Sorensen will help fill the void created by Arne Engels' sale to West Ham United.

"There's some key positions that we still need a bit of work on in the next couple of days," Maloney said before Wednesday's Scottish Premiership visit by Aberdeen.

"There's certain things that Arne brought that we need to replace and the quicker we do that, it gives us just that extra dimension, extra speed, extra power within that midfield because I think technically we've got some brilliant players. I think we just need that slightly different profile, which we need in certain games.

"Kieran's started the season really well. You never quite sure how this season's going to go with all the World Cup guys because of such a short break. We need that back-up in that position. We need somebody to keep challenging KT.

"That's a position that we've really needed to fill and with the right type. We need the right profile of player in there."

Celtic targets arrive as transfer window closure nears - gossip

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

Maloney was asked about the possibility of Celtic signing 18-year-old Chelsea forward Shim Mheuka on loan and said "it's pretty difficult to talk about" prospective signings and "nothing's confirmed with anyone".

"Any signing in that striker area, it'll either transpire in the next 24, 48 hours, or we'll just go as we are," Maloney explained.

On Hatate, who has scored 33 goals in 191 Celtic appearances since joining in January 2022, Maloney commented: "He's a brilliant player.

"What he's done at the club has been really, really good. He's won many titles here.

"If he does move on then he'll remember how good a player he was for this club."

The Scottish transfer deadline is on Thursday at 17:00 BST, with the Europa League squad to be registered by Wednesday at 23:59.

"All the guys that we'd be looking to try and bring in, with that European deadline we want to try and get them in the squad if we can," Maloney explained.

"We'll be looking to strengthen that squad, particularly European squad for that deadline.

"Some really key positions in the squad, you're looking at three or four and, if there's anymore than that, that'll be really, the thinking of the club will be for the future."
