title: John Roberts draws a line with Trump — over history
description: “That construction is likely unlawful,” Roberts wrote in dissent with the court’s liberals as Trump’s ballroom moves ahead
fullText:
"The White House is not just any building."

So said Chief Justice John Roberts, who has often deferred to Donald Trump's executive authority, but on Monday separated himself from the president and fellow Supreme Court conservatives to protest the colossal ballroom project.

It was a rare dissent and remarkable break for the chief justice who has penned some of the most important opinions backing Trump, including the 2024 grant of immunity from criminal prosecution and last June's decision giving him power to fire the heads of independent agencies.

Still, the rhetoric was vintage Roberts.

His six-page dissenting statement was laced with regard for history and architecture in the nation's capital. He quoted Theodore Roosevelt and Winston Churchill as he extolled the value of iconic structures.

"'We shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us,'" Roberts wrote, lifting a page from a 1943 Churchill war speech.

To that, the chief justice added, "All the more reason to ensure that those responsible follow the rules in deciding what to tear down and what to build up at the People's House."

Roberts, who regularly tells audiences that he once intended to pursue a history Ph.D. rather than law degree at Harvard, touted the symbolism of Washington's historic architecture.

He observed that when Roosevelt in 1902 thanked Congress for the appropriations for the additions of the East and West wings, Roosevelt referred to "the stately simplicity" of the original architecture and the importance of preserving "such buildings as historic monuments which keep alive our sense of continuing with the Nation's past."

Throughout his opinion, the chief justice, who often shows pride in the Supreme Court's columned building, demonstrated his own regard for the aesthetic of the White House structure. (The court did not have its own building until 1935, more than a century after the construction of the White House and US Capitol.)

Yet, Roberts' position failed to make a difference and was costless, at least to Trump. Roberts' five conservative colleagues had a majority to allow the president to continue the ballroom construction that has been underway for nearly a year and nearing completion.

Still, Roberts' statement Monday adds another dimension to the chief's record as he has confronted Trump's audacious second-term agenda. The Trump cases have dominated the court's docket and will contribute to Roberts' own legacy.

While Roberts has greenlit many of Trump's policies, he voted last session against two of the most extreme: the sweeping tariffs imposed on foreign goods without congressional approval, and the attempt to limit birthright citizenship, a centuries-old practice that entitles any child born in the US to American citizenship.

Monday's case invoking American history also serves as a reminder of Roberts' position as chancellor of the Smithsonian Institution. The role is largely ceremonial, by virtue of his role as chief justice, yet he has overseen Smithsonian board meetings and witnessed the Trump administration's ongoing effort to reshape the nation's major public museums.

Trump's drive to transform the look of Washington in his image has included his move to inscribe his name on the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and to build a triumphal 250-foot arch. The arch is planned for the traffic circle between the Arlington National Cemetery entrance and the Lincoln Memorial.

The case was brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation. It contended that demolition of the East Wing and the construction of 90,000 square-foot ballroom and security structure required congressional approval.

Lower federal courts preliminarily sided with the Trust and let the case proceed. Judges found that the Trust had "standing" to sue because it had demonstrated a significant injury. The Trust pointed to a long-time Trust leader and member, Alison Hoagland, an architectural historian, who claimed her enjoyment of the White House had been harmed.

The high court majority declared her grounds insufficient, writing "mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury" to sue. The majority issued the opinion, per curiam, Latin for "by the court," as happens in such appeals that come to its emergency docket. None of those justices (Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett) signed any separate opinion.

To Roberts, there was nothing meager about Hoagland's claim. (Joining his opinion were liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.)

The chief justice emphasized her architectural credentials as he observed, "The White House is not just any building, and – when it comes to historic preservation – Hoagland is not just any person."

He noted that past court cases have found an injury when "esthetic interests" were asserted. He referred to a 1992 precedent in which, as Roberts described it, with lines from that prior case, "a desire to … observe an animal species like a particular crocodile, even for purely esthetic purposes was undeniably a cognizable interest for purposes of standing."

As for the case at hand, Roberts declared, "A historic preservationist such as Hoagland can be aesthetically injured in a concrete, particularized way by the transformation of a historic building that she frequently enjoys, just as an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys."

Monday's case turned on the standing issue alone – the majority said it was not ruling on the lawfulness of the ballroom project itself – but Roberts made clear his view of the entire enterprise.

He observed at the outset that Congress had explicitly prohibited construction on such federal property "without express authority of Congress."

"That construction is likely unlawful," he said, declaring that the usual appropriation for White House maintenance "likely does not authorize the President to use hundreds of millions of dollars in private donations to tear down the East Wing and construct a ballroom in its stead."

title: Chelsea goalkeeper Sanchez joins Como on loan
description: Chelsea goalkeeper Robert Sanchez joins Como on a season-long loan after losing his starting spot to new arrival Emi Martinez.
fullText:
Chelsea goalkeeper Robert Sanchez has joined Como on a season-long loan after losing his starting spot to Emiliano Martinez.

Sanchez started the Blues' 3-2 win against Fulham in their Premier League opener but allowed Josh King's shot to slip through his grasp at the near post during an error-strewn display.

Concerns over the Spaniard's performances led to Xabi Alonso's side signing Argentina's Martinez from Aston Villa in a £7.5m deal.

Martinez started Chelsea's 4-3 win against Brighton on Sunday - just hours after the club announced his transfer - while Sanchez was dropped from the matchday squad.

Sanchez, who was Chelsea's first-choice goalkeeper since joining from Brighton in 2023, made 112 appearances and won the Conference League and the Club World Cup with the Stamford Bridge club.

BBC Sport understands Como, managed by former Chelsea and Spain midfielder Cesc Fabregas, have an option to buy the 28-year-old at the end of the loan.

Man City agree £125m fee for Chelsea's Fernandez

Transfer deadline day: Fernandez nearing £125m move to Man City, Woltemade joins Juve

Sanchez's exit represents a remarkable turnaround in opinion at Stamford Bridge.

Those in charge at Chelsea had been keen to back Sanchez but he was deemed surplus to requirements after his mistakes against Fulham and the arrival of Martinez days before the transfer deadline.

The club also have Mike Penders, a £17m signing from Genk, among their options. The Belgian made his debut in the Carabao Cup victory over Luton Town last week and was on the bench against Brighton at the weekend.

Meanwhile, Como have also signed Italy international Moise Kean, 26, from Fiorentina on loan with an obligation to buy.

The former Everton and Juventus striker scored eight goals in 26 Serie A appearances for Fiorentina last season.

Como finished fourth in Italy last season and will feature in the league phase of the Champions League this term.

title: Taylor prepared for test rather than testimonial
description: Katie Taylor is preparing for a stern test from Flora Pili rather than a Croke Park testimonial on Saturday night as she seeks to sign off on her career in style.
fullText:
Katie Taylor is preparing for a stern test from Flora Pili rather than a Croke Park testimonial on Saturday night as she seeks to sign off on her career in style.

Over 54 years will have passed since Muhammad Ali headlined the last boxing event at the home of the Gaelic Athletic Association.

Just as 'The Greatest' blazed a trail in a career that transcended sport, Taylor has done likewise.

Elevating women's boxing to heights never experienced or perhaps expected, the 40-year-old will make her final walk in front of 80,000 fans with the opportunity to become undisputed champion at light-welterweight once again.

It is all set up for the glorious farewell, and while talk about ring-walks and musical entertainment is a feature of fight week in Dublin, Taylor is looking no further than her 29-year-old French opponent, who is perfect through 12 fights and holds the European and IBO belt.

"I'm trying not to think about it as I have a job to do," Taylor, whose record stands at 25-1, said at Tuesday's news conference when the subject of the overall event was raised.

"It's too dangerous a sport to have your body in the ring and your heart out of it, thinking of retirement.

"I have a job to do, and I'm very much focused on that job. The most important part of Saturday night is I get my hand raised, so it's business as usual for me.

"I've a live opponent in front of me, so it won't be a walk in the park. She is here to win ... a young, undefeated fighter. It will be a tough fight, but that's when I'm at my best."

There is truth to that final statement as her best performances have come when the danger was at its greatest: in the victories over Amanda Serrano, the rematch against Chantelle Cameron and in a 2020 rematch against Delfine Persoon which came 14 months after a much tighter battle in New York.

Pili, perhaps not keen on brash statements, has arrived in Ireland with braided hair in the colours of the French flag, and while few outside of her camp are predicting the upset, there is a quiet confidence.

"We're all aware of the task ahead but have the whole of France behind us, so we will be proud to take on Katie," said Pili, who is aware there is everything to gain should she spoil the party.

"I've nothing to lose and everything to win. I'm the underdog, and there is no pressure on me, so I will give everything I can from the first bell and take home all of these belts."

Taylor's sole career defeat came at the hands of Cameron in Dublin back in 2023 - a loss she later avenged to become undisputed champion in a second division - so there is certainly a realisation this is not a foregone conclusion on Saturday.

Undoubtedly, Cameron - whose only defeat came in that rematch against Taylor - has proven herself as a bona fide elite fighter, a status Pili is yet to reach.

While promoter Eddie Hearn is predicting "one of the greatest moments Irish sport has ever seen" on Saturday night, that will only fully come to pass should Taylor prevail.

"She's got to focus on the fight, because this girl's decent," said the Matchroom boss.

"I'm not saying she's got the pedigree of Katie Taylor, but Katie's 40 years old. She's [Taylor] fighting a young, strong girl who likes to trade, and so does Katie, who's IBO world champion, European champion, a decent amateur who can become undisputed herself on Saturday.

"She [Taylor] was saying, 'I need to prepare myself for war here', because she can't walk out, then get in the ring, and then it just passes you by, because that can happen.

"It will be an all-out war, because it's the only way she knows how to fight. She's not going to try to box and move because she'll want to leave it all in the ring."

Taylor is certainly making all the right noises in that regard and has been as methodical as ever in camp.

While she accepts it is "hard to prepare yourself for a moment I haven't experienced before" in terms of the overall occasion, she is determined to add one final glorious chapter to an already remarkable legacy.

"I'm not sure how I'm going to feel, but it will be a special night," she added.

"I'm going to walk to the ring, focus on the fight, as there will be plenty of time after to reflect on this amazing career, should I get my hand raised.

"I wouldn't be human if I didn't think of it all and think of all the little girls who may be at a boxing event for the first time.

"In my mind's eye, I think of one of those girls who might fall in love with this beautiful sport and may even surpass my achievements, all because of one amazing September day in Croke Park. I can't wait to hear those stories."

title: Tronchon edges thrilling sprint to win Vuelta stage 10
description: France's Bastien Tronchon triumphs in a thrilling bunch sprint to win stage 10 of the Vuelta a Espana.
fullText:
France's Bastien Tronchon won a thrilling bunch sprint to take stage 10 of the Vuelta a Espana.

The Groupama-FDJ United rider held off Magnus Cort Nielsen and Thibau Nys to cross the line first in a photo finish, with Wout van Aert edged off the podium.

With a kilometre of the 184.7km route from Alcaraz to Elche de la Sierra remaining, Astana's Yevgeni Fedorov and Xabier Azparren of Q36.5 broke clear of the peloton.

However, they were caught just before the line with Tronchon timing his sprint to perfection to claim the stage victory.

"I launched my sprint and I just finished it on the line, but I wasn't sure if there was some guys in front or not, so I did not put my hands in the air," Tronchon said.

"That's crazy, I can't believe it. The last two days were really hard for me and today I was good, and I said to [team-mate] Guillaume [Martin] go full gas until you die and I take the win, so it's crazy."

Spain's Enric Mas, riding for Movistar, retains the red jersey as leader of the general classification, more than a minute clear of nearest challenger Primoz Roglic of Red Bull-Bora-hansgrohe.

British rider Oscar Onley of Netcompany Ineos is fourth, two minutes and two seconds down on Mas.

Wednesday's 11th stage from Cartagena to Lorca is 153.8km and is largely flat so, despite a category three climb up Morron de Totana, should suit the sprinters.

title: Red Bull hire Aston Martin engineer McCullough as head of racing
description: Red Bull have head-hunted former Aston Martin performance director Tom McCullough to become their head of racing from 2027.
fullText:
Red Bull have head-hunted former Aston Martin performance director Tom McCullough to become their head of racing from 2027.

The 50-year-old Briton is a replacement for Gianpiero Lambiase, who is moving to McLaren to become their chief racing officer at an unspecified time by 2028.

Red Bull said in a statement that they "looked forward to the wealth of experience and expertise he will bring to the role" when he joins at the beginning of 2027.

McCullough, a highly respected figure in F1, spent more than a decade at the team now known as Aston Martin, through its previous guises as Force India and Racing Point. Before that, he worked at Williams and Sauber.

In January 2025, a restructure led to him being moved off the F1 race team and to their performance technologies division.

The new role effectively runs all aspects of the race team under team principal Laurent Mekies.

It remains to be seen whether his appointment will ease the path to Red Bull and McLaren negotiating a settlement that allows Lambiase to leave earlier than currently stated.

Lambiase has become well known as Max Verstappen's race engineer, and for the direct and unfiltered relationship between them through their team radio messages.

title: Man City agree £125m fee for Chelsea's Fernandez
description: Manchester City agree to pay a British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.
fullText:
Manchester City have agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.

Fernandez joined Chelsea from Benfica in 2023 for a then-British record fee of £107m, with his latest switch matching the £125m that Liverpool paid for Alexander Isak also on transfer deadline day last summer.

The clubs have been negotiating over the past 24 hours and have now reached an agreement.

Fernandez, 25, will now undergo a medical ahead of signing a long-term deal at City. Personal terms will not be an issue.

Argentina international Fernandez worked with City manager Enzo Maresca during the Italian's reign at Chelsea.

Maresca is keen to work with him again after losing a host of midfielders this summer.

Fernandez was not involved in Chelsea's 4-3 Premier League win over Brighton on Sunday or their 2-0 Carabao Cup victory against Luton three days earlier, as reports in Argentina suggested he asked to be left out of the squad.

Chelsea set a deadline of 17:00 BST on 14 August for clubs to make offers of £120m or more, in an attempt to end uncertainty before the start of the 2026-27 season.

It is the second time this summer that City have broken their own transfer record, following the £116m arrival of Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest.

Fernandez becomes the fourth player to move to a Premier League club for a fee of at least £100m this summer - following Morgan Rogers (£117m) to Chelsea, Bradley Barcola to Liverpool (£123m) and City's signing of Anderson.

Transfer Deadline Day: Fernandez set for joint-British record £125m move to Man City

Man City sign Ndiaye from Everton for £65m

Everton agree to re-sign Grealish on loan from Man City

Four midfielders have departed Etihad Stadium this summer - Tijjani Reijnders joined Saudi Arabian club Al-Qadsiah for £52m, Barcelona signed Rodri for £65m, Nico Gonzalez made a £52m move to Newcastle and Bernardo Silva departed earlier in the summer before joining Real Madrid as a free agent.

City have also sold Savio to Tottenham for £75m, and will receive £60m from the London club next summer when Omar Marmoush's loan move is made permanent.

City have reinforced by signing 18-year-old midfielder Ayoub Bouaddi from Lille for £86m, Brazilian winger Allan Elias for £34m, plus winger Jeremy Monga and goalkeeper Geronimo Rulli for more modest fees.

Their total summer outlay could rise further with Everton winger Iliman Ndiaye set to join after the clubs agreed a deal worth up to £65m.

Chelsea had hoped to keep Fernandez earlier this summer but he has been pushing to leave the club since March, and wouldn't change his mind.

Fernandez had been targeting a move to Real Madrid, but the Spanish club ultimately issued a statement to rule out making an offer.

The deal represents the second-biggest sale in Chelsea's history after the one that saw Eden Hazard join Real Madrid in 2019, and means they are set to register a Premier League record for income generated from player sales.

Fernandez's departure, alongside the recent £65m deal that took Nicolas Jackson to Aston Villa and Liam Delap's £50m move to Nottingham Forest, has accelerated a staggering summer of sales now expected to be worth over £400m.

It is a substantial increase on the previous record of around £300m set by Chelsea last season.

Chelsea needed to trim their squad - they are out of European competition this season after finishing 10th and ended last season without a trophy.

title: Superb England crush Ireland with record ODI chase
description: Maia Bouchier's stunning century helps England women seal their record one-day international chase of 282 to beat Ireland in the series opener.
fullText:
First ODI, Uptonsteel County Ground, Leicester

Ireland 281-5 (50 overs): Lewis 69 (89), Hunter 62 (90), Stokell 54* (48)

England 283-4 (38.1 overs): Bouchier 104 (95), Dunkley 73 (61); Murray 3-58

England won by six wickets; lead series 1-0

England's new era started with a dominant six-wicket win over Ireland as they cruised to their record chase of 282 in the first one-day international.

Opener Maia Bouchier struck a stunning 104 off 95 balls to secure England's highest chase in women's ODIs with 11.5 overs to spare.

Bouchier added 143 for the first wicket with Sophia Dunkley, who made 73, which laid the perfect platform before the centurion holed out to long-on with just 59 runs needed.

Alice Capsey and Freya Kemp made light work of those remaining runs with a quickfire stand of 54 off 38 balls to put England within touching distance, Capsey hitting the winning boundary to finish unbeaten on 41.

Ireland were poor with the ball and sloppy in the field, but nevertheless it was a brilliant start for England's transitional batting line-up, which is without the recently retired Heather Knight and Tammy Beaumont, and in the absence of injured captain Nat Sciver-Brunt.

Despite their struggles in the field, Ireland earlier impressed with the bat to post 281-5, with half-centuries for captain Gaby Lewis, Amy Hunter and Rebecca Stokell.

Lewis and Hunter added 136 for the second wicket before Stokell's counter-attacking knock of 54 not out from 48 balls provided a late boost, as England's bowlers lacked threat in the middle overs, without Lauren Bell and Sophie Ecclestone, who are being rested.

It looked a competitive total at the halfway mark, but on a flat pitch offering little assistance for the bowlers, the gulf in class and experience was stark in the second innings.

The three-match series continues at Derby on Thursday.

'It's an unknown' - Capsey takes England gloves for first time

Both Bouchier and Dunkley are familiar faces in England shirts, but neither has really nailed down a place in the ODI XI despite plenty of opportunities.

But with the retirements of Beaumont and Knight, two of England's finest, head coach Charlotte Edwards is building towards next summer's Ashes with places up for grabs in the top order.

Edwards and the batters know tougher tests will come - only Orla Prendergast in Ireland's line-up offers a similar threat to the world's best bowlers - but both Dunkley and Bouchier made their cases at the first time of asking.

Bouchier started watchfully, making just eight off her first 19 balls, before a flurry of boundaries off medium-pacer Jane Maguire in the sixth over kickstarted her knock.

England reached 72-0 in the powerplay, with Bouchier playing second fiddle to Dunkley, who was brutal against Ireland's wilting bowling attack in a 47-ball fifty - her fastest in ODIs.

Dunkley was caught and bowled off Cara Murray in the 20th over but Bouchier held her nerve. She took ownership as Jodi Grewcock, the new face in England's line-up, looked nervous for her nine before finding the perfect company from Capsey's proactive approach.

Bouchier looked disappointed when she was caught at long-on after a lapse of concentration, but Kemp and Capsey ensured her efforts were not wasted - the former whacked 36 off 22 to show the power of England's rapidly-improving depth, with five batters missing from the team that started the 50-over World Cup semi-final last year.

Though there are concerns for Ireland's bowling as the series continues, it was a promising start to the series for their batters as England's own bowling attack looked unthreatening without the class and experience of Bell and Ecclestone.

Wong struck early to dismiss Alice Tector for 11 with assistance from a fine one-handed catch from Capsey, who is deputising for Amy Jones as wicketkeeper and showed promised with the gloves. But overall Wong was too inconsistent, bowling five wides in her spell.

Stand-in skipper Charlie Dean held things together with 2-44 but it was a tough outing for young left-arm spinner Tilly Corteen-Coleman, who bowled seven wicketless overs for 53 as the pitch offered little.

Ireland are heavily reliant on Lewis and all-rounder Prendergast, and when the latter fell for 19 after Lewis' knock of 69, there was a worry that their solid platform would be wasted.

But Stokell's dynamic knock appeared to take England by surprise as she struck the ball cleanly down the ground with regularity, and she even had to celebrate reaching fifty twice after the umpire mistakenly gave her runs for a boundary that had come off her pad.

She did eventually reach the milestone in a fifth-wicket stand of 84 with Leah Paul, but England's approach showed they would have needed a total beyond 300 to be challenging.

With two games to go, it feels like further records could be broken - especially if England are tasked with batting first.

title: Brughmans joins Liverpool in deal worth up to £30m
description: Liverpool have secured the signing of teenage goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans for the start of the 2027-28 season.
fullText:
Liverpool have completed the signing of 18-year-old goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans from Belgian side Genk in a deal that could be worth up to £30m including add-ons.

Brughmans has agreed a six-year contract with Liverpool and will remain at Genk on loan this season before moving to Anfield ahead of the 2027-28 campaign.

The Belgian keeper, who is 6ft 7in, has started all four of Genk's games this season and has represented his country at youth level.

BBC Sport understands that there is an initial fee alongside follow up payments and the figure of around £30m is at the top of what can be achieved.

Liverpool have Alisson, Giorgi Mamardashvili, Freddie Woodman and Vitezslav Jaros as their goalkeeping options, but with Alisson's contract expiring next summer and Mamardashvili's future looking uncertain, Brughmans will be an option from the summer of 2027 onwards.

The deal for Brughmans came about as a result of work from Liverpool's global talent department that is led by Matt Newberry.

Earlier this year, they signed Senegal's Mor Talla N'diaye and Austria's Ifeanyi Ndukwe after the teenage centre-backs both impressed at the U17 World Cup in Qatar, while goalkeeper Armin Pecsi and midfielder Samuel Martinez have both joined in the last 12 months from Hungary and Colombia, respectively. Pecsi is spending this season on loan at TSV Hartberg in Germany.

title: Sunderland sign Spurs defender Danso on loan
description: Sunderland have signed Austria defender Kevin Danso from Tottenham on a loan deal until the end of the season.
fullText:
Sunderland have completed the signing of Austria defender Kevin Danso from Tottenham on a loan deal until the end of the season.

The deal will cost the Black Cats £2.5m and will be made permanent next summer - for a fee of £22.5m - if Regis Le Bris' side stay in the Premier League.

"I'm really happy to be here and I can't wait to get started," said Danso.

"Sunderland is a big club with huge ambition, and I'm excited to be part of what we're building this season."

The 27-year-old - who made 52 appearances for Spurs after signing from RC Lens in January 2025 - will bolster Sunderland's squad ahead of their first European campaign since 1973.

Danso's exit from Spurs comes as Roberto de Zerbi's side close in on a move for Chelsea defender Tosin Adarabioyo.

The 2025 Europa League winners had a bid accepted for the former Fulham and Manchester City defender on Monday night.

Adarabioyo, 28, came through the ranks at the Etihad before joining the Cottagers on a permanent deal in 2020.

In 2024, the defender joined Chelsea following the expiry of his contract with Fulham.

Since moving to Stamford Bridge, Adarabioyo has made more than 70 appearances for the Blues across all competitions, winning the Conference League and Club World Cup.

Tottenham are also close to sealing a deal for Chelsea attacker Mykhailo Mudryk before Tuesday night's deadline.

title: Man City sign Ndiaye from Everton for £65m
description: Manchester City sign winger Iliman Ndiaye from Everton in a deal worth up to £65m.
fullText:
Manchester City have signed winger Iliman Ndiaye from Everton in a deal worth up to £65m.

The deadline day move for the Senegal winger, 26, is worth £60m plus a further £5m in add-ons.

"I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this," said Ndiaye, who has agreed a five-year contract at the Etihad Stadium.

"City are one of the best clubs in the world and I've seen them win everything as I've grown up. To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands.

"It's not always been easy in my career, but I always had the belief that I could play for a team challenging for the biggest prizes and now I'm here."

Ndiaye made 74 appearances and scored 21 goals for Everton since joining them from Marseille in 2024.

Tottenham had agreed terms with Everton on Friday night for Ndiaye, when it looked as though Richarlison would move the other way in a separate transfer.

However, sources indicated Richarlison failed to agree personal terms with his former club and as a result, Spurs were unable to proceed with the Ndiaye transfer.

The move comes on the same day City agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.

The Argentian international is set to become City's eighth summer arrival with Enzo Maresca's side having also signed Elliot Anderson, Geronimo Rulli, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Allan Elias, Jeremy Monga and Pierce Charles.

title: Ukraine dissects Russia’s Zircon missile as Moscow leans on harder-to-intercept weapons
description: A Ukrainian official says Russia's growing use of harder-to-intercept missiles marks a dangerous new stage as Patriot interceptor stocks run low.
fullText:
Ukraine's military intelligence published a detailed breakdown of Russia's Zircon missile.

The assessment reveals its components, speed, manufacturers, and foreign-made parts.

Russia has leaned more on hard-to-intercept missiles as Ukraine has gotten better at stopping other threats.

Ukraine's main military intelligence agency published a breakdown of Russia's Zircon missile, a weapon Moscow has increasingly employed in its intensifying strikes.

Russia has been investing heavily in advancing its missile arsenal, upgrading systems and making them harder for air defenses to intercept. That reaction to Ukrainian air-defense wins now represents a major challenge as interceptors run low.

On Monday, Ukraine's GUR, the country's military intelligence agency, shared details on Russia's 3M22 Zircon missile, including its components and production.

It also provided details on the main manufacturer NPO Mashinostroyeniya, a Russian defense company that is part of the Tactical Missiles Corporation, and foreign parts used in the weapon, which included some made by US companies. The disclosure also named more than 70 companies and dozens of people involved in its production.

In its new assessment, the GUR referred to Zircon as a ballistic missile, a departure from Russia's description of it as a hypersonic cruise missile. New details published by Ukraine describe it as a two-stage ballistic missile featuring a solid-fuel booster and a solid-fuel sustainer for flight.

Cruise missiles and ballistic missiles differ in how they fly and reach their targets. Ballistic missiles typically climb on a ballistic trajectory before descending at high speed toward their targets, while cruise missiles are jet-propelled and fly lower within the atmosphere.

Ukraine's assessment challenges Russia's long-standing characterization of the weapon.

The GUR also assessed that the Zircon is slower than claimed, with a maximum speed of Mach 6.8. Russia claims that the missile can reach speeds of Mach 9.

Russia has previously touted the Zircon missile as one of its "invincible" hypersonic weapons. It first used the missile against Ukraine in February 2024. At that time, Ukraine estimated that Russia had around 40 stockpiled.

The arsenal has since grown, though estimates vary, and Russia has increasingly fired these missiles in strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, leaning harder on more advanced missiles as Ukraine has demonstrated it can intercept other Russian systems.

"Since we learned to shoot down more than 90% of cruise missiles and drones with gasoline piston engines, Russia has decided to rely on ballistics and jet drones," Yehor Cherniev, the deputy chairman of the Ukrainian parliament's national security, defense, and intelligence committee, told Business Insider.

Russia did not immediately respond to Business Insider's request for comment on Ukrainian assessments of its weapons and motives.

Cherniev said that Ukraine assesses that Russia has reduced production of Kinzhal missiles because of accuracy issues and instead focused on producing Iskander and Zircon missiles. Russian forces have ramped up ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine this year, including debuting a new upgraded variant of its Iskander series, the Iskander-1000, earlier this summer.

These ballistic missiles are more difficult for Ukraine to intercept, and Russia's growing reliance on them comes as Ukraine struggles with shortages of critical air-defense interceptors. Ukraine relies on the US-made MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile system to confront Russia's more difficult missiles, but it has warned that interceptor stocks are running low.

"This is a new and extremely dangerous stage of the war, which requires us to be more effective in the fight against high-speed jet drones, as well as additional assistance from the United States in the form of PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems," Cherniev said.

title: Lake Ontario is now Lake America. Residents of Trump-voting Ontario have thoughts.
description: ONTARIO, N.Y. - Serafino Rosso lives in a big home in this tiny town overlooking the Great Lake it’s named after. When President Donald Trump renamed the lake, Rosso thought: Why stop there? “I would ...
fullText:
ONTARIO, N.Y. - Serafino Rosso lives in a big home in this tiny town overlooking the Great Lake it's named after. When President Donald Trump renamed the lake, Rosso thought: Why stop there?

"I would like it if they changed the name here to the Town of America: The Town of America on the Lake of America," Rosso, a 41-year-old telecoms manager, said proudly while standing outside Ontario's lone grocery store. "It makes me feel really patriotic. It felt Canadian before."

Trump escalated a trade war with Canada with his executive order renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America, sparking an international outcry. Even in places where most people love Trump, not everyone is on board with upending centuries of tradition to score points in an improvised trade war.

Nowhere is the issue more salient than the place called Ontario on the U.S. side of the lake. Republicans have mixed feelings about the rebrand in this lakefront Upstate New York community of 10,000 in a county that Trump has decisively won in his presidential runs.

"I don't think the lake's name should be changed because it's history," Dave Rupp, who runs the town's liquidation store and voted for Trump in 2024. "And I don't like changing history."

Ontario was originally named Freetown in 1807 in honor of the first settler, Freeman Hopkins. Then it was renamed Ontario less than a year later for the lake forming its northern boundary.

Today, Ontario has seven churches, two Dunkin' restaurants and a town hall. Stickers on pickup trucks read "Respect our farmers."

The influence of agriculture on the town shapes how people view Trump's feud with Canada. Some hope his sweeping tariffs on Canadian goods, including agricultural products, would ultimately help American farmers by easing competition across borders.

The executive order states that the lake's name change is meant "to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements." But while signing the order, Trump told reporters that Canada "has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly." Trump similarly ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed the Gulf of America last year in a dispute over immigration.

Cassandra Tylenda, who voted for Trump, said that she tries to avoid politics, but she hopes that Trump's tariffs help local farmers. Her grandparents had a dairy farm, and she has a small farm where she grows and cans peaches and pickles.

But that doesn't mean she wants to rename the lake.

"I like Lake Ontario better," Tylenda, 29, said while bartending at a local sports bar and restaurant. "But there's nothing I can do about it," she added with a shrug.

The name change has also struck a nerve with the president's detractors.

Rochester Mayor Malik Evans, who leads the heavily Democratic lakefront city west of Ontario, dismissed Trump's executive order as a "publicity stunt."

Serena Eaton, who lives near Ontario, said the renaming was a "distraction" from the Epstein files, the war in Gaza and other issues the Trump administration is facing.

"America doesn't just own the lake," Eaton, 24, said. "I'm not going to call it Lake America. But my town is really redneck. I'm sure a lot of people will just switch their brains off and tune out sensible reason."

Charles Smith, a member of the Cayuga Nation who lives just outside Ontario and has lived in New York and Canada, noted the lake's name has deeper roots far preceding American politics.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney highlighted that same history in response to Trump's order, explaining in an X post that the lake's name comes from "the Wendat word Ontari'io, which, appropriately, means 'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.'"

"It's been Lake Ontario for a very, very long time," Smith, 59, said in an interview outside of one of the two Dunkin' restaurants. "And it will always be Lake Ontario."

The name is already being erased from some official sources. The U.S. Interior Department is updating its geographic systems to reflect Lake America as the new name. Over the weekend, Google Maps changed Lake Ontario's name to Lake America for U.S. users. But Canadians will continue to see the name Lake Ontario.

Some cheered on the revision. After an afternoon riding his boat on the newly christened Lake America, Frankie Amalfi, 33, praised Trump's leadership in taking on what he saw as Canada's unfair trade advantage.

"He will tell you right off the bat that Canada's been getting us for years," Amalfi said as he reclined in Ontario Beach Park's Marina in Rochester. "He doesn't let them walk all over us."

Soaking in the last of the day's sun to the sound of the lapping lake, Amalfi reveled in how the new name annoyed its detractors and referenced a statement made by the president while signing the executive order.

"We have the Gulf of America, the Lake of America," Amalfi said. "All we need now is the Ocean of America."

title: US and Iran trade strikes, and other Mideast news
description: The United States military said Tuesday that it struck new targets in Iran as hostilities flared after a month without military action.  Iran fired missiles and drones in response, Iranian semiofficia...
fullText:
The United States military said Tuesday that it struck new targets in Iran as hostilities flared after a month without military action.

Iran fired missiles and drones in response, Iranian semiofficial media said. The Fars and Tasnim news agencies, seen as close to Iran's security forces, reported late Tuesday that Iran had launched such operations.

Here's a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.

U.S. Central Command said the new strikes come after Tehran tried to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and U.S. service members in the region.

U.S. President Donald Trump warned in a social media post that if Iran retaliates, "they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings."

On Sunday, the U.S. military said it struck rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran responded by launching missiles at U.S. sites in Jordan, which were intercepted, while the United Arab Emirates said it stopped an Iranian drone over its waters.

After the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, Iran established a chokehold on the strait, through which a fifth of the world's traded oil passed in peacetime, slowing ship traffic to a trickle. That has roiled the global economy, raising prices worldwide for energy and other goods.

While Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian has long favored a negotiated end to the war, the most powerful force in Iran remains the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, which is pressing for greater concessions from the U.S., including Iranian control over the strait and financial compensation for the war. Those conditions would likely be unacceptable to Washington.

The State Department renewed a regionwide travel alert for the Middle East as hostilities between the U.S. and Iran resumed.

"Due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation," the department said in a blanket advisory covering all countries in the region. The language is similar to that used in previous warnings that came before a lull in combat activities and said Americans in the Mideast should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential travel disruptions.

Iran has been working with Oman, which sits on the south side of the Strait of Hormuz, on a framework for managing shipping traffic, though it remains unclear whether the plan would be acceptable to the U.S.

Other Gulf nations have stressed the need to reopen the strait unconditionally.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom's de facto ruler, met with Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, on Tuesday, according to the Saudi Press Agency, which said the two discussed "ongoing efforts to maintain regional security and stability," but did not mention the strait specifically.

The United Nations nuclear watchdog has been unable to inspect nuclear facilities in Iran affected by the 12-day war in June 2025, according to a confidential report by the U.N. watchdog circulated to member states and seen Tuesday by The Associated Press.

The International Atomic Energy Agency said in its report that therefore it "cannot provide any information on the current size, composition or whereabouts of the stockpile of enriched uranium in Iran."

Israel said it detained a senior Hamas security official in a special forces raid in Gaza City on Tuesday. The operation killed at least four people, including two children, hospital officials said.

In a joint statement, Israel's military and national security agency said the operation targeted the head of Hamas' internal security.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement that the detainee, who he did not name, is "one of the most senior Hamas leaders" and that he was most recently "engaged in efforts to restore Hamas's governance in Gaza."

Yemen's state security said that Islamic State spokesperson Abu Huzayfah al-Ansari was killed in Yemen in a joint operation by Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and the Yemeni counterterrorism forces.

He was killed at dawn Tuesday while he was hiding in a house in Seiyun city in the Yemeni province of Hadramout, according to a security statement published by state-run SABA news agency.

A U.S. official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said there was no U.S. military involvement in the operation.

— Ben Finley contributed from Washington.

The British military's United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre said it received reports of an attack on a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, and a second report involving a nearby tanker.

The UKMTO said a tanker was hit by three projectiles Monday on its way out of the Persian Gulf through the strait east of Oman. In the second attack the same day, the center received a report "involving a tanker and military forces" off the coast of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attacks.

This version corrects the item on the U.N. confidential report to reflect that the nuclear watchdog says it has been unable to inspect facilities affected by the 12-day war in 2025.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AI will create ‘hundreds of thousands’ of new jobs—including for people who want to ‘make things with their hands’
description: Unlike Bill Gates, the billionaire Nvidia CEO is bullish that AI will create more jobs than it eliminates—and skilled trade professionals stand to benefit.
fullText:
As executives race to boost productivity and automate work with AI, workers have been left to ponder an existential question: How much work will actually be left for humans? But if you ask Jensen Huang—the CEO of the world's most valuable company, Nvidia—the answer is plenty.

"Don't forget the chip plants that are being created—packaging, computer plants, and all of the AI factories being created—hundreds of thousands of jobs are being created as we speak," Huang said on Fox Business last week.

The billionaire was responding to newfound concerns from Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates about AI's disruption of the workforce. Gates warned in a letter last week that the technology is being underestimated and could ultimately lead to massive unemployment. Huang, meanwhile, has remained optimistic that AI will create more jobs than it eliminates.

"Everybody's job changes," Huang said. "Some jobs will be eliminated. Many new jobs will be created. If you go back and look at history and technology, revolutionary technology comes along, incredible advances come along."

Huang added that white-collar jobs aren't going anywhere anytime soon, while predicting a major boom in the skilled trades. The massive infrastructure buildout fueling the AI boom is already driving demand for hundreds of thousands of skilled plumbers, electricians, technicians, and other six-figure earning workers needed to build and maintain the technology.

"Having a large population of skilled labor and people who build things, that make things with their hands, is tremendous for the United States," the 63-year-old said.

Huang, who has an estimated net worth of $180 billion, has been calling for greater attention to the skilled trades for months.

"If you're an electrician, you're a plumber, a carpenter—we're going to need hundreds of thousands of them to build all of these factories," Huang told Channel 4 News in the U.K. in September 2025. "The skilled craft segment of every economy is going to see a boom. You're going to have to be doubling and doubling and doubling every single year."

At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, this past January, Huang added the world is on the cusp of what he calls the "largest infrastructure build-out in human history," which will create "a lot of jobs."

While Huang often frames that buildout as beneficial for the broader U.S. economy, it is also increasingly critical to Nvidia's own growth. The company's chips power the data centers at the heart of the AI boom, and building those facilities requires far more than advanced semiconductors. It takes thousands of skilled workers to get power plants, electrical systems, and cooling infrastructure online.

title: The light is blinking red on Trump messing with the 2026 election
description: It should surprise nobody that the president who tried to overturn the 2020 election based on lies — and didn’t seem to mind his supporters rising up violently on January 6, 2021 — might try to monkey...
fullText:
It should surprise nobody that the president who tried to overturn the 2020 election based on lies — and didn't seem to mind his supporters rising up violently on January 6, 2021 — might try to monkey with the 2026 midterm elections.

It remains to be seen whether President Donald Trump's efforts to interfere in the 2026 election will actually work.

But recent developments should serve as a reality check that he's trying, with potentially ugly results.

First, CNN reported exclusively that the Department of Homeland Security is surging efforts to find supposed voter fraud in a handful of states.

While that might not sound shocking in and of itself, there is plenty about it that's irregular.

The effort involves using an arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement called Homeland Security Investigations, which typically handles other crimes like human trafficking and drug smuggling.

But mostly, the reason it should raise eyebrows is because of the proximity to the 2026 election, now just a little more than two months away. As CNN's Priscilla Alvarez, Tierney Sneed and Gabe Cohen note, the federal government typically avoids such "overt" investigatory actions so close to an election. The reason is that mere allegations that haven't been thoroughly examined could influence the election.

But when it comes to Trump and alleged voter fraud, that's a feature rather than a bug.

Trump has spent a decade trying and failing to substantiate his claims of widespread fraud. In his first term, he launched a voter fraud commission that folded with little to show. His campaign paid people to find widespread fraud after the 2020 election, to no avail.

What the administration has produced of late is a lot of manufactured smoke.

That includes its bogus claim about 250,000 noncitizens being registered to vote in just four states. It also includes a highly unorthodox unsigned report from the US Census Bureau last month claiming tens of thousands of noncitizens voted in the 2020 presidential election. (Experts have decried both claims.)

The DHS effort would seem to be geared toward promoting such claims, given the department's purview.

But if other efforts to find widespread voter fraud didn't produce anything substantive, the odds would appear slim that DHS will change that in just two months.

Of course, producing ironclad evidence of fraud probably isn't the point. The Trump administration's goal appears to be seeding more doubt — and possibly even creating a pretext for more federal intervention in the election (which we'll get to).

The other big development this week was an unnamed federal whistleblower issuing a major warning about the Trump administration's new system for verifying mail ballots. The system has devolved into what workers describe as a "sh*t show" that could lead to mass disenfranchisement of mail voters, the whistleblower says

The whistleblower report, released by Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, builds on concerns previously expressed by election officials that the system has not been sufficiently tested ahead of the 2026 midterms.

According to the whistleblower, if even a single ballot envelope scan in a large batch of ballots doesn't comport with the information in the system, the US Postal Service won't deliver the entire batch until the discrepancy is resolved.

It remains to be seen whether the system will actually be used; the issue is the subject of extensive litigation. But Trump — who has himself voted by mail in Florida — has long decried mail voting. And because of that, it skews substantially toward Democrats.

In other words, if mail voters are disenfranchised, it could disproportionately hurt Democrats.

These developments only add to the warning signs about what might lay ahead.

Trump in March signed the executive order giving the USPS an unprecedented role in screening mail ballots. By June, CNN reported that the administration was planning to threaten not to deliver mail ballots for states that failed to turn over their voter lists to the federal government.

(Even some red states have resisted turning over those voter lists.)

And a few weeks later, Trump declined to rule out precisely such a scenario. In an interview, he left open the possibility of declaring a national security emergency to institute a series of voting changes that the GOP-controlled Congress has failed to pass, including limiting mail voting.

And last week brought a particularly striking scene.

Amid longstanding concerns that the Trump administration might overzealously insert itself into the voting process, the Republican governor of a dark-red state accused Justice Department election monitors of "aggressive" behavior while observing that state's primary election.

Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon asked his state's attorney general to investigate, while adding: "I don't like the federal government coming in and taking our votes."

Trump has previously expressed regret for not seizing voting machines after the 2020 election.

It's impossible to say which of these developments might lead to concrete action or problems ahead of the 2026 election. Trump tends to throw things at the wall, and sometimes he backs off when they prove impractical. Other times, his and his team's efforts prove half-baked or ham-handed. The courts could get in his way on things like his plans for mail ballots.

But as CNN's Zachary B. Wolf wrote this weekend, there are a bevy of potential nightmare scenarios in play ahead of this fall's midterms.

And with Trump's party staring down a difficult election that could give Democrats at least one chamber of Congress — and thus could sap Trump of power over his final two years as president — it's worth taking those possibilities seriously.

History and recent developments suggest Trump is capable of plenty.

title: Pennsylvania police officer charged with voluntary manslaughter in killing of college student
description: Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin Steele said Upper Pottsgrove Police Cpl.  Sean Farrell, 58, is charged in the Aug. 23 death of Glenwood Earl Pysher IV.  The prosecutor said the officer had l...
fullText:
NORRISTOWN, Pa. (AP) — A Pennsylvania police officer who fatally shot a 22-year-old college student, who had ended up at the wrong house late at night and was waiting for friends to pick him up, has been charged with voluntary manslaughter, a prosecutor said Tuesday.

Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin Steele said Upper Pottsgrove Police Cpl. Sean Farrell, 58, is charged in the Aug. 23 death of Glenwood Earl Pysher IV. The prosecutor said the officer had less-than-lethal options and did not need to resort to shooting Pysher during the encounter.

The Montgomery County Detective Bureau investigated the shooting and reviewed footage from Farrell's body-worn camera, the district attorney's office said in a news release.

"The investigation found that Cpl. Farrell had less-than-lethal options on his utility belt that he did not employ, including a taser. At the time of the shooting, the officer was a safe distance from Pysher behind a car, and the victim had his hands in the air and did not possess any type of weapon. Mr. Pysher was not a threat. This is not a legal use of deadly force, leading to the charge of Voluntary Manslaughter," Steele said in a news release.

An attorney for Pysher's family issued a statement thanking the prosecutor.

"The family is grateful for the work of the Montgomery County District Attorney's office and they are looking forward to justice in this horribly tragic, preventable and reckless conduct that took the life of their son," said attorney Ken Fulginiti.

Farrell turned himself in to the Montgomery County Detectives on Tuesday. Magisterial District Judge Kathleen Rebar set bail at $75,000, and Farrell must turn in all weapons to the state police as a condition of his release, a spokesperson for the district attorney's office said. He has a preliminary hearing set for Sept. 10.

Farrell was the first officer on the scene after a resident called 911 to report someone trying to break into the back door of a home. Farrell's body-worn camera showed the officer walking down the driveway with his gun drawn, using its light to illuminate the way, the release says.

Standing behind a car in the driveway, Farrell saw Pysher on the home's patio, near the back door. Farrell yelled, "Police, let me see your hands." Then he yelled, "Hands up, hands up now, drop to the ground."

Pysher is seen on video raising his hands as he began walking toward the officer and continuing to walk in that direction as the officer yelled, "Drop to the ground," the release said. Farrell again yelled, "Drop to the ground," then yelled, "Stop or I'll..." But before he finished the sentence, Farrell fired two shots, hitting Pysher twice in the chest, the district attorney's office said.

Pysher was 17 to 20 feet (5 to 6 meters) from the officer when he was shot, the release says.

The investigation found that Pysher had been out at several bars earlier in the evening to celebrate a friend's 21st birthday. A designated driver drove the group to the home of the person whose birthday it was around 11 p.m., and Pysher left about half an hour later to walk half a mile to another friend's house to keep drinking but ended up at the wrong house, the release says.

Pysher's father has said he believes, based on what his son's friends have told him, that his son tried to enter what he thought was his friend's house.

"He tried to open the doorknob and obviously startled the homeowner," Glen Pysher told The Associated Press last week. "From what we understand, he announced, 'Hey! Open the door!' because he thought he was at his friend's house."

His son then sat down on the back porch and contacted his friends, who realized he was in the wrong place and set out to find him, the father said.

Brumback reported from Atlanta.

title: Canada's Carney says US needs to start being serious before trade talks can resume
description: OTTAWA, Sept 1 (Reuters) - The U.S. needs to start being serious and stop trying to be tough before talks on a possible trade deal with Canada can restart, Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters on
fullText:
OTTAWA, Sept 1 (Reuters) - The U.S. needs to start being serious and stop trying to be tough before talks on ‌a possible trade deal with Canada can restart, Prime Minister ‌Mark Carney told reporters on Tuesday.

Canada walked away from negotiations on an agreement to avoid ​additional U.S. tariffs on August 21, saying the American side had made unacceptable last-minute demands.

Since then U.S. President Donald Trump has declared that Lake Ontario should be renamed Lake America, described Canada's leaders as "the worst" he ‌has to deal with, ⁠and repeated assertions that Canada is ripping off the U.S.

He also posted an AI-generated meme showing Canadian geese with ⁠Trump's distinctive hairstyle marching under a U.S. flag.

Carney said there was still a chance to strike a mutually beneficial trade deal that respected Canadian ​sovereignty.

"And when ​the Americans stop doing memes, stop ​throwing shade, stop trying to ‌be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions," Carney said, adding that recent U.S. actions were "not constructive."

U.S. officials have challenged part of the Canadian narrative as to why the talks collapsed, saying there was a good deal to be ‌had on the table. Carney said Ottawa ​had never felt the proposed terms would ​be adequate, especially when it ​came to the highly integrated auto sector.

"The attitude of ‌the United States... has been one ​that the core ​Canadian industries either would be subsidiaries, effectively, of the United States industries, or (Washington) would put in place terms where those industries ​would be gradually wound ‌down in Canada and wiped out," he said.

"Of course, we're ​not going to accept those terms."
