title: I work on AI at Amazon. My biggest career regret is waiting years to build a reputation outside the company.
description: An Amazon employee shares how he built a reputation outside the company — and why the effort can sometimes feel like a second job.
fullText:
Abhinav Bohra's biggest career regret: letting his work stay behind Amazon's walls.

He developed a list of rules for himself to follow as he built greater professional visibility.

Going public opened doors — but added an AI "learning tax" to his nights and weekends.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Abhinav Bohra, a senior applied scientist at Amazon. He's in his 30s and lives in Seattle. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

For most of my career, everything I built lived and died inside Amazon.

I joined Amazon in 2019 as a data scientist and eventually became a senior applied scientist in 2024. My background is in AI recommendation systems, and I work on models that help determine which products shoppers see on Amazon.

While I was building a reputation inside the company, I wasn't building much of one outside it. People in the industry outside Amazon were publishing research papers on the same problems I was solving, and I never joined the conversation.

I eventually realized that without a public record of my work, I was missing opportunities to speak at industry events, serve on conference committees, and build a reputation that could help me if I ever needed to find a new job. When it came to professional opportunities outside Amazon, it felt like I was starting from zero.

The lesson I learned was that internal reputation doesn't travel. My biggest career regret is how long I took to show up outside the company. I'd be a few years further along if I'd realized this sooner.

At first, I was hesitant to publish externally. I treated anything within a mile of my day job as radioactive, which meant I shared nothing publicly. There are processes for publishing company work externally, but they can require documentation and review, and I didn't want to go through that process.

Eventually, I realized I could do external work without using the company's proprietary data or information. The data was proprietary, but my ideas and research were not.

Take a problem I worked on a few years ago: How do you train a good AI model when you have almost no labeled data? Research teams everywhere hit that wall.

I developed some rules for myself. If a problem exists in published research, it's a conversation. If it only exists in our codebase, it's not. Nonpublic data, internal metrics, customers, code, roadmaps, and unreleased products are all off the table. If I'm still unsure, I won't share it.

Business Insider is speaking with tech workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations.

Share your story by filling out this form.

It surprised me how much meaningful technical discussion was still possible without revealing anything proprietary.

In 2021, I started taking steps toward sharing more of what I was learning, and I published my first research paper around a year later. Publishing papers opened the door for me to start reviewing other researchers' work and helped me build relationships in the industry.

Eventually, I was able to land some external speaking opportunities. I think having published research and experience reviewing other researchers' work is what made the difference.

Posting on LinkedIn became part of my strategy, too. I shared my research, technical ideas, and conference work. I wasn't trying to become an influencer — I was just trying to build a professional identity that wasn't tied to a single employer.

In recent years, the going-public bet has started to compound in ways I can actually point to rather than just describe.

I've since become a Challenge Co-Chair for ACM RecSys 2026, an international conference focused on recommender systems. I reached out, explaining my background, research, and reviewing record, and said I was interested in serving on the organizing committee.

After the organizers reviewed my background and we spoke on a call, I was appointed. Reaching out got me considered, but the work behind the initial email is what made the opportunity possible.

I've also joined a mentorship program through Johns Hopkins, where I advise early-stage ventures on AI and technical strategy.

Building an external reputation isn't only about having accomplishments to put on my résumé.

I think the work I was doing inside Amazon would have gotten better faster if I'd started engaging with people outside the company earlier.

When you explain your thinking in a paper or on a conference stage, you're writing for people with no context and no reason to be polite. The weak spots in your work show up fast. Strangers make the best reviewers precisely because they owe you nothing.

Over the years, my outside work has made me more confident at Amazon. I think the biggest change was becoming more comfortable contributing an idea before I had every detail perfectly figured out.

AI learning can become an unofficial second job. It's valuable and exciting, but it also blurs the boundary between professional development and personal time. Outside my day job, I spend evenings and weekends researching retrieval and recommendation systems and submitting research papers on the topic.

I enjoy the work, so I don't want to frame it as purely negative. But it does affect work-life balance. There are evenings or weekends when I should probably be disconnected, but I end up spending time on AI because I know the field is moving quickly.

AI creates opportunity, but it also creates a learning tax. For people working close to the field, continuous learning has quietly become part of the job, even when it happens outside the job.

There's value in having a public record of your work if your career ever takes an unexpected turn. Life can be uncertain. There could be layoffs. There could be a difficult job market that makes it hard to find a new job.

You don't want to spend years developing tools, solutions, and expertise, leave a company, and feel like you're starting from scratch because everything you built was proprietary and you can't share it.

My advice to other people working in tech is to make sure you have a profile outside your company that allows someone to understand the value you can bring.

That doesn't mean sharing proprietary information or violating an NDA. There are other ways to build a public record. For me, that means publishing independent research, speaking at industry conferences, reviewing other researchers' work, and becoming involved with organizations related to my field.

title: It's taken me a long time to process Olympic experience - Raygun
description: Australian Olympic breakdancer Rachael Gunn - known as Raygun - tells BBC Sport about the aftermath of her extraordinary experience at the 2024 Olympics.
fullText:
Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.

Thrust into an environment full of experienced athletes, it dawned on Gunn, whose professional background is as a university lecturer, what she had got herself into.

Known as Raygun when competing, she was about to take part in the breakdancing event - or breaking - which was making its Olympic debut.

"I felt like an imposter," said the 38-year-old breaker, during a new Netflix documentary about her experience at the Games.

She describes how she reacted when she saw someone she recognised from the Olympic team.

"I just could not stop crying... I had a panic attack. 'What am I doing? What have I done? Should I be doing this?'" she said.

Just a few hours later, she was sailing down the River Seine alongside the rest of the Australian cohort, waving to onlookers.

Less than a fortnight after that, her Olympic journey was over. Gunn failed to win any of her three round-robin battles at the Games, but walked away pleased with how she had acquitted herself.

"Finishing my last round, the world champion Nicka [Dominika Banevic] gave me props for my moves, the MC celebrated my stuff and the vibe was just generally good," Gunn told BBC Sport.

What she hadn't anticipated was that one of her performances, in which she debuted some unconventional moves including a sprinkler and a kangaroo hop, had gone viral.

There were memes. There was a sketch on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Adele referenced the performance in one of her concerts. Chris Hemsworth defended Gunn in an interview with Jimmy Kimmel. At one point in August 2024, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese even felt moved to speak out, praising Gunn for having "a crack".

"It was pretty wild the way I became a topic of conversation in spaces I never thought I would be," said Gunn.

Alongside the teasing, there were more sinister forces brewing, including conspiracy theories about nepotism - for instance that Gunn's husband and trainer, Samuel Free, had been on the selection committee when she qualified to represent her country at the Games, when he hadn't been.

"It was really tough when mine and Sammy's credibility, ethics and motivations were being called into question," Gunn said.

"You could just spend 30 seconds researching and find plenty of sources to debunk these conspiracies, but that's not how people use the internet anymore."

That new-found scrutiny took a toll on Gunn's mental health.

"I felt like my whole life was just kind of crumbling before me.. .and I was just trying to get through the day," she says in the documentary.

In the process of making a film about that time, however, she feels that she's been able to regain some agency.

"It's taken a long time for me to process what happened," Gunn told BBC Sport.

"It's really exciting for me to finally have a voice again."

After it was announced that breaking would be included at Paris 2024, Gunn qualified to represent her country via the Oceania Breaking Championships in Sydney in 2023.

"I've never participated in anything of such high stakes before. It was all international judges, but I was relieved and excited when I qualified. And then the next whirlwind happened," she said.

Quickly, she realised that she would have to start living like an athlete.

Gunn gained a scholarship at the New South Wales Institute of Sport in February 2024, which allowed her to begin a strength and conditioning programme.

"That was great, but also overwhelming because I was training with people who had been doing that stuff since they were kids," she said.

In the midst of her training, the documentary reveals that Gunn's mother suffered three brain aneurisms. Gunn herself began a course of anti-depressants to help with feelings of anxiety.

The film portrays how it began to dawn on her what she had taken on when she entered competitions in the run up to the Games.

"That's when it first starting occurring to me that I was going to be going up against world champs and people who had been winning competitions on big stages for years and years, but I was still going to go out there and do my best," she says in the documentary.

In that context, Gunn decided to play to her own strengths with a creative gamble, developing a routine that paid cheeky homage to her Australian roots.

"I was aware that I was never going to beat my competitors on athleticism," she explained.

"For me, my strength is creativity. With that being one of the [judging] criteria, our thinking was, 'why don't we put all our eggs in that basket and really try and wow them? Maybe we can make a moment.'

"We never, ever expected the impact it might have."

The documentary reveals that head of the Australian Breaking Association, Lowe Napalan, only assisted Gunn's training "a handful" of times in the build-up to the Games, owing to the amount of administrative work taking up his time.

That meant that he only saw Gunn's controversial routine for the first time just before she performed at the Olympics.

"I was there side-stage," Napalan says in the film.

"I had to not have a face of shock."

It was reported in November 2024 that the furore around her Olympic performance had led Gunn to quit breaking.

"I don't know where that came from," Gunn said.

"I wouldn't let what happened take dancing away from me. I love breaking, I'll always break, I'll always be a part of the community."

Her hope is that the release of the upcoming film can help shift the conversation.

"It feels nice to lay it all out there and now be able to look to the future. I'm actually excited about what's to come, which is the first time for a while," she said.

title: Girl who allegedly recorded livestream of Islamic center shooting charged with murder
description: The North Carolina teen was indicted on three counts of first-degree murder.
fullText:
A 17-year-old girl from North Carolina has been indicted on murder charges for allegedly aiding the suspects in the deadly attack on the Islamic Center of San Diego by disseminating a livestream of the May shooting and releasing their writings, officials announced on Monday.

The teen, Sarah Santiago, is being charged as an adult with three counts of first-degree murder and one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder, according to an indictment filed Monday in Forsyth County.

A lawyer for Santiago maintained the teen's innocence.

"The discovery in the matter has not been released to me for specific evidentiary comments," the attorney, Alan Doorasamy, told ABC News. "Suffice it to say, this matter is sub judice and at this time I can confirm that my client is innocent of all these charges."

San Diego Islamic Center shooting suspect apparently posted video of attack: Sources

Three men were killed in the May 18 shooting at the Islamic center, which is home to a school where some 140 children were playing in the back at the time gunfire erupted, prosecutors in Forsyth County said.

Two suspects in the attack -- 17-year-old Cain Clark and 18-year-old Caleb Vazquez -- were found dead in a vehicle nearby, authorities said.

"When I looked at this, the facts of this case, the evidence of this case, I realized that what we really had was the purpose and plan of Vazquez and Clark that day was twofold -- number one, it was to kill as many people possible on that day, and secondly, they wanted this -- their carnage and destruction -- recorded, live-streamed and disseminated out," Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O'Neill said at a press briefing on Monday, referring to the two suspects as "domestic terrorists."

Santiago was allegedly communicating with the suspects on Signal leading up to the attack and was among three people who watched the livestream, according to O'Neill. She is also accused of providing a Sonnenrad patch, depicting a neo-Nazi symbol, that Vazquez allegedly wore during the attack, according to the indictment.

"This was not a single-day plan. This had been building up," O'Neill said.

O'Neill said that while Santiago was not in California at the time of the attack, she can be charged with murder in North Carolina because she is accused of aiding and abetting the suspects.

Security guard at Islamic Center of San Diego hailed as a hero

"When someone has credible knowledge that a crime is going to be planned or to be committed, particularly any act of violence, the law requires them to come forward and report it," FBI Charlotte Special Agent in Charge Reid Davis said during the presser. "Failure to do so is not only irresponsible, but it can also be a crime."

The indictment also alleges that Santiago conspired with the two suspects to attack worshippers at a Jewish temple and African-American students at a high school.

The teen, a student in the Winston-Salem Forsyth County school system, was arrested last week ahead of the grand jury indictment, according to O'Neill. He said authorities decided to act because it was close to the start of the school year and holy holidays.

"We looked at the carnage that had occurred in California, and quite frankly, this is a student in the Winston-Salem Forsyth County school system, and the thought of her going back to school, or with the weekend approaching, holy days approaching, we didn't know what she was capable of," O'Neill said. "It was frankly too great a risk to wait until a grand jury could decide."

The investigation is still ongoing, Davis said.

Amin Abdullah, Nadir Awad and Mansour Kaziha were killed in the shooting at the Islamic Center. O'Neill hailed them as heroes.

"The men who died at the mosque that day were men of courage, sacrifice and faith," he said. "They saved countless lives that day."

title: He was dragged 60ft under a bus - now he's fighting for a UFC contract
description: Liam McCracken will compete for a UFC contract on Dana White's Contender Series on Tuesday, three years after he was left fighting for his life when he was hit by a bus.
fullText:
The first thought Liam McCracken can remember having after he woke up was that he was glad to be alive.

On Tuesday, the Briton is set to compete for a UFC contract on Dana White's Contender Series in Las Vegas, but just three years ago he was fighting for his life.

While out on a run near his home in Liverpool, McCracken stepped out into the road without properly checking for oncoming vehicles, and was hit by a bus.

The 25-year-old from Liverpool says he didn't see the bus until the last moment, and was dragged underneath it for 18 metres (60ft) and seven seconds before it stopped.

A couple who saw the incident found McCracken under the bus unconscious and bleeding heavily. They thought he was dead.

If not for passers by on the main road, among them a paramedic with life-saving equipment in their car, McCracken says he would probably have bled to death before an ambulance arrived to take him to hospital.

The accident left McCracken with four fractures in his back, two slipped discs in his neck, three broken ribs, a broken pelvis, a broken nose, a ruptured anterior cruciate knee ligament, a torn meniscus and multiple other wounds.

For a long time he worried he might never walk or compete again - but remarkably, he will fight Mexican lightweight Silvestre Sanchez on Tuesday.

"For the first few days I wasn't caring about anything else other than the fact that I was alive," McCracken tells BBC Sport.

"I have a little daughter and apparently the people who found me said that was the first thing I kept speaking about when I regained consciousness.

"I kept asking about my little girl while I was on the floor getting seen by people. The main thing was I was glad to be alive."

McCracken says the incident and recovery which followed were some of the most difficult moments of his life but he tells the story in good humour.

"My girl had just turned one. One of the funniest things is she wasn't walking at the time and literally a day or two after it happened she started walking. I stopped being able to walk while she'd just learned to walk," says McCracken.

McCracken was not only unconscious but was being burned by the engine of the bus - but the driver could not turn the ignition off because the suspension would have dropped, with the vehicle potentially crushing him.

A pedestrian had to help the driver guide the bus away from McCracken before anyone could tend to him.

"A woman was with me holding my hand on the floor and then loads of people started coming over," said McCracken.

"They came over and saw to me straight away which basically saved my life because I was losing a lot of blood. I had to get multiple blood transfusions."

At the time McCracken had won five of his six fights as a professional and was being touted as a future UFC star, but he had a long road ahead of him if he was to make his dream a reality.

McCracken says there were serious doubts whether he would fight again because doctors said he might need a metal rod in his back, which would have ended his career.

However, after multiple X-rays, it was determined he would not need it.

"It was a long road and very up and down and if things along the way went a little different, I wouldn't be back fighting," he said.

"It was the longest six months of my life and I finally started to get somewhere when I had to have knee surgery, which is a massive surgery.

"So I had to basically start all over again. That was one of the hardest parts."

After multiple operations followed by hours of physio and training, McCracken eventually returned to action almost two years after the accident.

"It was very up and down and I did some stupid stuff like trying to jump back into training when I wasn't ready to," said McCracken.

"Obviously it was stupid - but the mentality I had was I wasn't going to let it stop me, and that's what's allowed me to get back in a way."

McCracken won via a rear-naked choke againstg Brazil's Jhon Bryan on his return, but says his performance was not up to his usual standard because he was not fully focused on his opponent.

"It was like I was in a film. I was looking around thinking 'how is this happening'?" said McCracken.

"I didn't ever think it was going to happen. It felt like I was having an out of body experience."

McCracken says the accident has "made him a lot more grateful for life" and the phrase "you could get hit by a bus tomorrow" has taken on a whole new meaning for him.

"When it actually happens to you it's real. I could go from this interview now and cross the road and my life could be over, so it makes you much more grateful," said McCracken.

"You're grateful for just being able to walk because I know what it's like to have your dignity stripped from you."

McCracken started MMA as a hobby as a youngster but with two children now, he sees the sport as a way to provide "financial freedom" and to give his family a life that he "wouldn't be able to do working a normal job".

A statement win on the Contender Series would provide a large step towards achieving his goal, as well as completing a remarkable recovery from a near-death experience.

"I feel really good and after everything I've been through I feel like I'm ready, mentally, for anything in life," said McCracken.

"The fight doesn't feel too big. I feel like I would have had impostor syndrome a couple of years ago, whereas now it feels right and I'm ready for it."

title: Juventus agree to sign Woltemade on loan from Newcastle
description: Juventus agree a season-long loan deal for Newcastle United forward Nick Woltemade.
fullText:
Juventus have agreed a season-long loan deal for Newcastle United forward Nick Woltemade.

The Italian side had been one of a number of clubs from the continent interested in signing the 24-year-old before Tuesday's deadline.

Woltemade - brought to Newcastle from Stuttgart in August 2025 - is now set to travel to Turin for a medical after a £3.5m deal was struck. It does not include an option to make it permanent.

Although Woltemade came off the bench to set up Yoane Wissa's goal in Newcastle's 2-0 win at Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday, the club's £69m record signing has only started one of new manager Matthias Jaissle's first three games to date.

Juventus had been in the market for a forward as Jonathan David looks set to join Atletico Madrid on loan.

They had also been talking to Manchester United striker Joshua Zirkzee, whose proposed move to Fiorentina was not completed.

However, Juventus feel Woltemade is a better fit and, crucially, is also cheaper. In addition, the loan agreement does not include the obligation-to-buy clause Manchester United wanted with Zirkzee.

BBC Sport previously reported that Newcastle's move for Lille forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo could pave the way for Woltemade to join the Serie A side.

Fernandez-Pardo flew into Tyneside on Monday evening to finalise a move worth up to £55m.

title: Apollo to Repackage $9 Billion Oneok Stake Into Debt Deal
description: Apollo Global Management Inc. is looking to turn another multibillion-dollar corporate equity deal into investment-grade debt it can sell to investors.
fullText:
(Bloomberg) -- Apollo Global Management Inc. is looking to turn another multibillion-dollar corporate equity deal into investment-grade debt it can sell to investors.

Nvidia to Invest $3.5 Billion in Chipmaker MediaTek

Trump Urges FCC to Probe Media Polling, Punish NBC Moderator

Forget GLP-1 Stocks, Baldness Drugs Are Wall Street's Next Goldmine

Trump's Venezuela Oil Grab Reprises Industry's Neocolonial Past

Bessent Faces Credibility Test Selling 'American Growth Agenda' to G20

Apollo's $9 billion stake in Oneok Inc. will be treated as permanent equity by the borrower, allowing the Tulsa, Oklahoma-based energy company to raise capital without adding conventional debt or pressuring its credit rating. The deal was announced Sunday.

Apollo is aiming to structure the deal so securities backed by its holding can get investment-grade ratings, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing confidential information. The capital is treated as a minority equity investment that's subordinated to the firm's existing debt. Apollo then slices that up into levels of seniority, some of which can be rated investment grade.

Such deals are partially placed with Apollo's insurer Athene and third-party insurers, as well as with other Apollo and client funds.

The move highlights a strategy that the New York-based alternative asset manager has been fine-tuning across a growing number of deals. Such transactions provide companies with capital that behaves like equity and avoids the leverage and risk of downgrades that come with raising debt. It's another example of how Apollo has become a go-to financier for large corporations.

Apollo has completed more than $100 billion of such transactions, including those with Intel Corp., Vonovia SE, Germany's largest residential landlord, Anheuser-Busch InBev, Air France-KLM and BP Plc. Apollo said its pipeline for deals, which include similar types of structures, tops $100 billion.

The Oneok deal was originated by Apollo's Capital Solutions business, which is led by executives including Jamshid Ehsani.

Apollo's lending model hinges on constant growth and a steady supply of highly rated assets to feed Athene's balance sheet. The firm now oversees more than $1 trillion.

The new deal will help Oneok buy Brazos Midstream Holdings' natural gas operations in West Texas for $4.4 billion and repay debt. Apollo's investment sits in a newly created holding company, ONEOK Holdings, that is structurally subordinate to ONEOK's existing senior debt, which is rated BBB.

title: Dortmund agree loan move for Arsenal's Nwaneri
description: German club Borussia Dortmund agree a deal with Arsenal to sign Ethan Nwaneri on a season-long loan.
fullText:
Borussia Dortmund have agreed a deal with Arsenal to sign Ethan Nwaneri on a season-long loan.

The German club are set to sign the forward, 19, after losing new signing Giannis Konstantelias to a significant knee injury sustained during Saturday's 2-0 win over Hamburg.

Nwaneri - who Dortmund tried to sign last summer - is now expected to arrive in Germany for a medical and to complete the move before the Bundesliga transfer deadline at 19:00 BST.

BBC Sport revealed earlier this month that Arsenal would prioritise loan offers for Nwaneri, who they do not want to sell.

The Gunners academy graduate has attracted interest from clubs across the Premier League and Europe during this summer's window.

With manager Mikel Arteta having an abundance of attacking talent, Nwaneri would probably have had limited opportunities at Arsenal this season, and there is a sense at Emirates Stadium that the teenager would benefit from increased game time at another club.

title: Everton agree deal to re-sign Grealish on loan from Man City
description: Everton agree a deal for Jack Grealish to return to the club on a season-long loan from Manchester City.
fullText:
Everton have agreed a deal for Jack Grealish to return to the club on a season-long loan from Manchester City.

The 30-year-old is set for a medical at the Toffees, with his move expected to be completed before Tuesday's 23:00 BST transfer deadline.

Grealish spent a large chunk of last term at Everton under a similar arrangement, scoring twice and providing six assists in 20 appearances, before sustaining a season-ending foot injury in January.

The England winger had been linked with other teams - including his boyhood club Aston Villa - but his preference was to return to Everton, whose chief executive Angus Kinnear told BBC Radio Merseyside had "remained in contact" with Grealish.

With Toffees winger Iliman Ndiaye, 26, expected to complete a £65m switch to City, the Merseyside club want to bolster their attacking options before the deadline.

Everton also look to be closing in on the signing of Monaco and USA forward Folarin Balogun in a £40m deal.

However, their bid to re-sign Brazil striker Richarlison from Tottenham appears to have stalled over personal terms.

Grealish, who joined City from Villa for £100m in August 2021, has made two appearances for Enzo Maresca's side this season.

He came on as a substitute in their Community Shield defeat by Arsenal before coming off the bench in a win against Bournemouth in their Premier League opener.

Grealish did not figure in a 4-1 victory at Crystal Palace on Friday.

Meanwhile, Everton's Scotland defender Nathan Patterson could move to Serie A side Torino before Tuesday's transfer deadline.

Talks are under way between the clubs about a deal for the 24-year-old. It is not yet clear whether any transfer would be on loan or a permanent move.

Everton are next in action on Sunday, when they host Manchester United in the Premier League (14:00 BST).

title: Georgia cop kills beloved pet donkey in his own pasture as heartbroken owner demands justice: 'We miss him'
description: A Georgia family is demanding justice after police fatally shot their beloved pet donkey, HeeHaw, while searching for a missing child who was later found.
fullText:
A Georgia police officer shot and killed a family's beloved pet donkey after officers searched the animal's pasture in search of a missing child who was later found at a nearby church.

Hannah Israel, 30, said officers entered her family's property in Rockmart, Polk County without warning at about 12:45 a.m. on Sunday while looking for the missing child when they noticed the baby donkey named HeeHaw.

"They claimed he ran up to them braying and they thought they were in danger and shot and killed him after trying to Taze him," Israel wrote on Facebook. "HeeHaw was shot and killed in his OWN pasture for doing what donkeys do. Alerting to a stranger. There is no way this is legal!"

She vowed to take legal action as she demanded justice for HeeHaw.

Police Dog Follows His Nose To Find Missing Autistic Teen Screaming For Help

"We are heart broken. He was my SON!!" she wrote.

"We miss him so much where is safe?? When my own baby was shot in his own home?" she added in another post.

A photo taken after the shooting showed Israel crying over her pet donkey, as the animal's eyes remained wide open as it lay lifeless on the ground.

"He would normally be standing right over there talking while I'm talking because he thought he could talk like a person could talk," Israel told 11Alive.

"Every time he saw somebody, he would run up and bray," Israel said. "And then do a really goofy sound, and because he loved people, and he thought he was a person. He slept in my bed for the first three months of his life," she added.

The Cedartown Police Department said the officer who shot the beloved baby donkey has been placed on paid administrative leave.

"The Cedartown Police Department has turned over the investigation of the animal shooting to the Georgia Department of Agriculture Law Enforcement Division for investigation and placed the officer involved on paid administrative leave while this investigation is ongoing," the department said in a statement.

Cedartown Police Chief Jamie Newsom said body camera footage exists, and he has viewed it, according to 11Alive.

"That search took them to the incident location where this very unfortunate and heartbreaking event occurred," Newsom said, according to the outlet.

Newsom said he understands the heartbreak that the family and the community are facing after the donkey's death.

"They're members of the human family, and I am too, and heartbroken," he said.

Dog Saved From Isis By Army Veteran 'Kidnapped' From Family Yard By Local Authorities

The Georgia Department of Agriculture's Law Enforcement Division was at Elsberry Farm on Monday investigating HeeHaw's death.

Israel created a GoFundMe to help cover legal costs related to HeeHaw's death. She said any donations left over would go toward the farm, care of the animals and a future HeeHaw foundation. She has raised more than $113,000 as of Tuesday morning.

"My bottle baby donkey 'HeeHaw' was killed in his own pasture on Saturday night by trespassing cops," she wrote on the fundraiser. "He was a loved member of our family and did many petting zoos and made many people smile."

She said she hired a lawyer but stressed that donations left over after legal costs would not be used for personal needs.

title: Abdul El-Sayed stands by criticism of fireworks, tells Americans to find other ways to 'show you love'
description: Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed appeared to defend his criticism of Fourth of July fireworks on "The Breakfast Club" radio show.
fullText:
Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed defended his past controversial comments about Fourth of July fireworks during a radio appearance Monday.

While appearing on "The Breakfast Club," El-Sayed was asked by host Charlamagne tha God about his previous support for defunding the police and criticism of firework celebrations on Independence Day. El-Sayed pushed back against the criticism.

"They're coming at me on fireworks," El-Sayed said. "I'm like, 'All right, first, if your whole conception of America is that it's fireworks, I'm so sorry. You don't have a complete conception of America. But even then, right, like what is it?'"

Washington Post Throws Cold Water On Dc Fireworks With Report Of 'Hazardous Air Pollution'

He continued: "I said, 'Well, every time we do a fireworks show, it destroys the air quality and people have asthma exacerbations and heart attacks the next day.' That's all I was saying. You know what I mean? I'm not saying we shouldn't have fireworks. I'm just saying maybe like there are other ways to show your love."

El-Sayed's comments follow a CNN report earlier this month that revealed that El-Sayed deleted or hid approximately 100 YouTube videos before launching his Senate campaign. Among them included a plea that Americans "please" find another way to celebrate the Fourth of July besides using fireworks, citing air quality and the risks to children and pets as reasons.

Socialist Candidates Can Delete Old Posts, But They Can't Erase Their Radicalism

The video allegedly included four reasons "why fireworks suck" and a chapter titled "Fireworks just aren't worth it: hear us out."

While appearing on "Hannity" earlier this month, Republican nominee Mike Rogers called out El-Sayed for his deleted posts and comments.

Abdul El-sayed Plays Down Hasan Piker Ties After Streamer's Viral Antisemitism Firestorm

"This guy spent hours hating on what most Michiganders would enjoy in their pastimes, and he should be held to account for that," Rogers said. "These are views that he held, that he was pretty strong about, but he knew that he had to delete them all… If people really knew who he was, they wouldn't vote for him."

Fox News Digital reached out to the El-Sayed and Rogers campaigns for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

title: Pakistan changes 'most shocking ever' - Afridi
description: Pakistan's decision to make dramatic changes to their squad during the series in England is the "most shocking decision ever", according to former captain Shahid Afridi.
fullText:
Pakistan's decision to make wholesale changes to their squad and coaching set-up during the series in England has been branded the "most shocking decision ever by a selection committee" by former captain Shahid Afridi.

The tourists have dropped seven players and called up five uncapped players, while head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and his assistant Umar Gul have been replaced by Pakistan white-ball coach Mike Hesson and former Australia seamer Ashley Noffke.

Pakistan, who were thrashed in the opening two Tests, face England in the third and final match of the series at Edgbaston, starting on Wednesday, 9 September.

"Not sure what is the logic or reasoning behind this decision!", Afridi wrote on social media.

"Even the replacements make no sense - T20 players have been included for a Test match in England?

"What is this thinking and approach? Why has the coach been axed after five Test matches?

"This is the most shocking decision ever by a selection committee which includes so many experienced selectors."

Pakistan drop seven players and release head coach

Pakistan to meet King Charles after Lord's controversy

Five of the players dropped - Muhammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman and Khurram Shahzad - have featured in the series so far, while Aamir Jamal and Muhammad Awais Jafar have been sent home without playing.

A total of seven players have been called up. Batters Saim Ayub and Abdullah Fazal have previous Test experience and join the quintet of uncapped newcomers.

Spin-bowling all-rounder Arafat Minhas, left-arm seamer Mohammed Imran Jr, wicketkeeper Said Baig and all-rounders Mohammad Imran and Razaullah have all received call-ups.

Ex-Pakistan captain Ramiz Raja, also a former chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm trying to convince myself this is all OK, but it is not.

"It just shows Pakistan cricket has hit a panic button."

Pakistan are scheduled to have an audience with King Charles at Clarence House this week in an engagement that was planned before the series against England began.

However, it is set to take place despite the series almost coming to controversial early end during the second Test.

At lunch on the first day, the PCB threatened to cancel the remainder of the match and tour because of an interview with the sons of Imran Khan that was broadcast by Sky.

Imran, the former Pakistan captain and prime minster, has been in prison for three years on charges of corruption, which he denies.

Pakistan ultimately completed the Test, with both captain Babar Azam and head coach Sarfaraz denying any knowledge of a planned boycott.

title: What does Norris deal mean for Piastri? F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the Italian Grand Prix.
fullText:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli will try to tighten his grip on the drivers' championship on home ground at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix at Monza.

However, the 20-year-old can expect to face a challenge from a resurgent McLaren and in particular Lando Norris, who has won the past two grands prix.

And Monza is of course also home territory for Ferrari, although the long straights of the historic circuit may not suit the characteristics of their car.

BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before round 13 of the 2026 season.

What does Lando Norris' new contract extension mean for Oscar Piastri? There clearly is some tension behind the scenes and this season his development performance-wise has clearly dipped. - Juha

There is no question that Oscar Piastri has not started this season as well as he did last.

In 2025, the Australian for a large part of the year appeared on course for a first world title, until his season unravelled somewhat in the final third.

This season, team-mate Lando Norris has won two races - and should have won a third in Miami.

Piastri has only looked in contention for a victory in Hungary, when Norris took his first win of the year.

After taking the lead when Norris made an error on the first lap, there was some bad luck involved in Piastri losing the lead to Norris, when he was delayed lapping Carlos Sainz's Williams.

But Piastri acknowledged it would have been difficult to hold Norris back if he had retained the lead because his pace on the hard tyres was weak. It became academic when he retired with a broken gearbox.

Although the qualifying head-to-head statistics between them do not make pleasant reading for Piastri - Norris is 12-4 ahead - on actual pace, there is not a lot to choose between them over one lap. Norris is only faster by 0.071 seconds on average.

It's fair to say, though, that Norris has been comfortably the more convincing race performer - hence the 55-point and three-place gap between them in the championship

There seem to be a few things at issue here.

One might be that Piastri has always been strong in high-speed corners. But the numbers of these that are grip-limited has reduced this year because the engines are often using them to charge the battery, something about which all drivers have complained. So that reduces a point of potential advantage for Piastri.

Second, the cars have less downforce than last year, and Piastri is less comfortable than Norris in low-grip conditions.

Finally, there is no question that Norris upped his game consistently over the course of the second half of last season to win the world title, and has continued to raise his level through this year. Without question, he is one of the drivers of the season so far.

Team principal Andrea Stella said at the last race in the Netherlands: "Last year, we had seen already with Oscar that, from a technical driving point of view, when the car has this low level of grip, like we saw last year for instance in Mexico or in Austin, he needs to adapt the way he drives, the way he thinks, the driving, his expectations.

"This requires a bit of mental effort, which gets him to lose a couple of tenths of a second because you sort of have to process rather than drive through pure instinct because what happens is what you expect.

"So it's one of those cases in which you have to adapt your natural driving style to the demand of the car. So it stays in the space of driving and in the space of the technical side of things. I don't think it has anything to do with any psychological kind of opportunity. This is purely technical."

Stella points out that the top three teams are very close in terms of performance, which means, as he puts it, "as soon as things are not optimised, then you may have a very significant positional loss - it's very brutal from this point of view".

Both McLaren and Piastri reject any suggestion that there might be tension in their relationship.

It's a fact, though, that McLaren wanted to sign Max Verstappen this summer, and that if they had it's virtually certain it would have been Piastri who was replaced.

That possibility has receded for now, with Verstappen's new contract with Red Bull. But that contract has performance clauses, and if Red Bull are still struggling next year, it may well be that McLaren have another go for Verstappen.

For now, Piastri is under contract to the end of 2027 at least, and will be focusing only on getting back to where he knows he can be.

Slow start makes me want to stay - Norris extends McLaren deal to 2030

Why are Mercedes choosing to take a grid penalty for Kimi Antonelli at the next race in Italy? Why not take it at a future grand prix to give Kimi a better chance for a home win or is this not a concern for Mercedes? - Michael

Mercedes have been quite open about the fact that Kimi Antonelli will take a new engine for the Italian Grand Prix, and with it a significant grid penalty that is likely to mean him starting at the back.

The reality is that early season reliability meant this penalty - for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts - was inevitable, and Mercedes have calculated that Monza is the best place to take it for Antonelli.

They have tried to make the decision on facts, and not let the emotion of it being his home grand prix enter into the equation.

This decision will be based partly on the fact that Monza has long straights, and so is one of the tracks where a new engine and its slight performance increase will translate most effectively into lap time.

But also important is Mercedes' analysis of how the engines in his 'pool' can be used most effectively over the remainder of the season

Team principal Toto Wolff said: "With Kimi, we are taking the full thing. In theory, our calculations say that it's the best track to take it. Obviously, algorithms don't take the nationality into consideration. I'm not ready to fight for a championship and get the best PR. That's what we're going to do."

Antonelli's championship lead is still very comfortable, at 59 points. So he can afford to be phlegmatic about this.

He says: "Of course, it's my home race and all that kind of stuff, but, you know, I think it's the best race to do so. So, I think it still will give me a chance to do a great result and bring home good points."

George Russell will have to take a penalty soon, too. This is most likely to be at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, for similar reasons to Antonelli's being at Monza.

Are Ferrari allowing emotion to get in their way? It's perhaps a stretch to say Ferrari can go on to win the title, but surely their best chance is backing the nearest challenger? Are they allowing the emotion of their attachment to Charles Leclerc, and his history with the team, to get in the way of making the clinical, ruthless decisions needed? - Alex

Presumably this question is a reference to the brief dispute between Charles Leclerc and the team at the Dutch Grand Prix, when Lewis Hamilton was coming up behind him on fresher tyres mid-race.

We dealt with what happened there in detail in last week's Q&A.

But in the context of the question, it's worth pointing out that they actually did ask Leclerc to move out of the way to optimise Hamilton's race in Zandvoort.

Ferrari operate a policy of equality between their drivers and only favour one over the other if it is obviously in the interests of the team.

That could work either way, and the most obvious time it would be employed is if a race victory was at stake.

Hamilton is their closest driver to the championship lead, at 59 points behind Antonelli. Leclerc is 28 points behind the seven-time champion - only four points further back than Lando Norris.

Hamilton and Leclerc have won one race each, and the qualifying battle between them is incredibly close.

Hamilton is ahead 9-7 on the head-to-head in races where a fair comparison can be made, but Leclerc is actually slightly quicker on average by 0.053secs.

Beyond that, the question seems to presume that the team would favour Leclerc emotionally. But why make that presumption?

Team principal Frederic Vasseur was instrumental in getting Hamilton to join Ferrari for 2025, but he has a long and close relationship going back many years with both drivers.

Why would he be emotionally connected to one more than the other, or consciously allow emotions to rule his management decisions?

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra and Sports Extra 2; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

Zandvoort is a great circuit and it's disappointing that they have pulled out of hosting the F1 grand prix for a second time. Is there any chance the circuit might return to the schedule some time in the future? - Lynne

In F1, one quickly learns to never say never, but the chances of the Dutch Grand Prix returning to the calendar seem remote for the foreseeable future.

The race was unique in that it owed its existence to the popularity of one driver - Max Verstappen.

The organisers did an impressive job to host a grand prix at a track that has many logistical challenges, in terms of both its location and its facilities, and to make it work financially for as long as they did.

It was highly popular with Dutch fans. But the event was privately run with no government financial support, and organisers decided that, as race fees went up, the risks that the event would not turn a profit were becoming too high.

This decision was influenced by the fact that there had been a slight decrease in interest in the last couple of years. Understandable, as the novelty wore off.

So organisers decided to end the event after a good run before any decline became more significant and they made a loss.

F1 has no shortage of events with which to replace it. Portugal and Turkey are both coming back to the calendar next year, for example.

title: A loss that feels different - Djokovic's future more uncertain than ever
description: After Novak Djokovic's latest bid for a historic 25th major title ends in tears in New York, where does the most decorated men's player of the Open era go from here?
fullText:
Be warned: Novak Djokovic has made a fool of those who have doubted him before.

Some questioned if the Serb would challenge for the sport's top honours again after he dropped out of the world's top 20 amid a two-year major title drought in 2018.

Djokovic proceeded to win four of the following five Grand Slams, doubling his tally of majors with 12 across the next six years.

But three years have now passed since he landed his men's record 24th major title at the US Open.

And, as the 39-year-old fought back tears mid-match on Sunday night, this latest loss in New York felt different.

Staring at a first opening-round Grand Slam exit since 2006, one of sport's all-time greats simply had nothing left, beaten 7-6 (7-5) 5-7 4-6 6-2 6-1 by Argentina's Navone.

For so long now Djokovic has not only defied time, but appeared to be improving with it.

That was evident at this year's Wimbledon, where he outlasted Felix Auger-Aliassime, 14 years his junior, in a five-set thriller that became the longest quarter-final in the tournament's history.

Even in his late 30s, Djokovic has been the one challenging Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, the new dominant forces in the men's game.

At the Australian Open in January, he ended Sinner's bid for a third-straight title in a sensational five-set comeback victory. He then led Alcaraz by a set in the final, before fading to a four-set defeat.

After early exits in Paris and New York, there is an inevitable sense that Melbourne was his best chance to secure an outright record 25th major triumph and cap a career unparalleled in every statistical measure.

Djokovic was despondent after the match, saying he "despised every moment I spent on the court for that".

"When it comes to the match itself, and the overall feeling of how I felt with my body and playing, it was really not enjoyable," Djokovic said.

"But, from the perspective of the crowd and support, it was incredible.

"I'm very sorry that I didn't perform as well as I should have, could have, or wanted - for them."

Djokovic in tears during US Open first-round exit

The four-time winner's shock first-round US Open defeat means:

Djokovic will drop out of the world's top 10 for the first time since July 2018

His record streak of 78 successive wins in first-round matches at Grand Slams is over

As is his perfect 37-0 record in the first two rounds at the US Open

He suffered a first-round exit at a major for the first time in 20 years, when the then 76th-ranked Serb lost at the 2006 Australian Open

Djokovic's refusal to disappear from contention on the sport's biggest stages has prolonged the final embers of the 'Big Three' era that captivated crowds for the best part of two decades.

But, for the first time in almost 24 years, the next world ranking update will have a top 10 missing at least one of Djokovic, Rafael Nadal or Roger Federer.

Nadal, a 22-time major winner, called time on his career aged 38 in 2024, two years after 20-time slam champion Roger Federer did so aged 41.

While Djokovic, who will turn 40 next May, is still going, they all share one thing in common - they each last won a slam aged 36.

Ken Rosewall remains the oldest men's singles slam champion in the Open era, winning the 1972 Australian Open two months after turning 37.

There is no doubt that the game has become far more physically demanding over the 54 years since.

Djokovic prevented Federer from breaking Rosewall's record when he saved two championship points to win the 2019 Wimbledon final, one month before the Swiss turned 38.

And early exits are still rare for Djokovic at the Grand Slams. He has reached at least the semi-finals eight times at the past 12 majors.

Up until now, Djokovic has not been as physically hampered as Nadal and Federer were in their final years on tour.

But despite feeling that he had made his best recovery from a slam in two years post-Wimbledon, Djokovic recently revealed his struggles with an ongoing health condition that causes particular issues in hot, humid conditions.

Djokovic dropped to his hands and knees and required a medical timeout in a surprise second-round loss in such conditions at August's Cincinnati Masters.

The New York humidity was largely irrelevant once the roof was closed after just seven games on Sunday night - but by then, Djokovic was already struggling.

He vomited and cramped during his four hours and 36 minutes on court, saying it felt as if his "whole body starts to collapse".

Since winning his last slam, Djokovic achieved his lifelong goal of winning Olympic gold at Paris 2024.

With that triumph - two months after knee surgery and three weeks after losing to the Spaniard in the Wimbledon final - Djokovic became only the fifth player to complete the career 'Golden Slam'.

Since then, his attention has been on breaking his tie with Margaret Court of 24 major singles titles.

He has slimmed down his schedule to prioritise the majors. In 2026 he has contested just seven tournaments - four Grand Slams and three Masters 1000 events - and his 21 Tour-level matches are his fewest in a season since 2004.

Reacting to Djokovic's defeat, former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "You can't substitute matchplay. You can't be walking into a Grand Slam on a hot and humid day and expect to get through a five-set match.

"I know he's super-human in many ways but it's going to catch up with you."

Djokovic has stated his desire to continue in the sport until the next Olympics, in Los Angeles in 2028.

It would be a fitting stage for his farewell - not least that it would be exactly a decade since his ability to still compete for the biggest prizes was first questioned.

Discussing retirement in his recently released documentary, Djokovic said: 'Why would I talk about retirement when I still keep proving to myself that I can still win?'

But, as of Sunday night, legitimate doubt has been cast on whether that remains true.

title: Pogačar eyes world championships after successful collarbone surgery
description: Tadej Pogačar underwent successful surgery on his broken left collarbone after his heavy crash at the Vuelta a España, his team doctor Adrian Rotunno said on Monday. The operation went well, Rotunno said, adding that the Slovenian star would remain in hospital for a few days for postoperative monitoring.
fullText:
Tadej Pogačar underwent successful surgery on his broken left collarbone after his heavy crash at the Vuelta a España, his team doctor Adrian Rotunno said on Monday.

The operation went well, Rotunno said, adding that the Slovenian star would remain in hospital for a few days for postoperative monitoring.

Pogačar would travel home as soon as he was able to, where he would begin his recovery and rehabilitation under the supervision of the medical team, Rotunno said.

The injury leaves Pogačar facing a race against time to compete at the road world championships in late September. Team manager Mauro Gianetti had said before the operation that Pogačar could still target the world championships, but that a firm assessment would depend on the surgery.

"Of course it wouldn't be easy to recover for the world championships," Gianetti said on the Vuelta rest day Monday.

Pogačar, who has won the world title for the past two years, suffered a heavy crash during Saturday's eighth stage of the Vuelta. He suffered a collarbone and cervical fracture as well as a concussion.

A broken bone typically takes about six weeks to heal, although cyclists have returned to competition after four weeks in some cases.

Gianetti said he had been deeply concerned immediately after the crash.

"I was a bit relieved when he stood. I said to myself: 'OK, he is standing, walking, he wants to continue.' But of course, that was not possible."

Pogačar had been hoping to win the Vuelta for the first time this year. The five-time Tour de France winner had previously ridden the Spanish Grand Tour only once, finishing third in 2019 at the age of 20.

He also hopes to compete at the world championships in Montreal, with the road race scheduled for September 27, and at the Tour of Lombardy on October 10. Pogačar has won the Italian one-day race, known as the "Race of the Falling Leaves," four years in a row.

title: Detroit Lions Sign OL Elijah Klein
description: The Detroit Lions are signing former Buccaneers offensive lineman Elijah Klein to their practice squad, adding an experienced blocker with versatility across the line.
fullText:
The Detroit Lions are adding some outside experience to their practice squad.

Detroit is signing offensive lineman Elijah Klein, according to Greg Auman. Klein spent the first two seasons of his NFL career with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers before being released during final roster cuts Sunday.

The move gives the Lions another developmental lineman with something Detroit clearly values: positional flexibility.

The Buccaneers selected Klein out of UTEP with the 220th overall pick in the sixth round of the 2024 NFL Draft. Tampa Bay viewed his ability to move around the offensive line as one of his strengths from the beginning, noting that Klein primarily played guard in college but also had experience at tackle. Tampa Bay's original Klein draft profile

That versatility continued in the NFL.

Justin Rogers of Detroit Football Network noted that the 6-foot-4, nearly 320-pound Klein has taken preseason snaps at right guard, left guard, center and right tackle over the past two years.

Klein has already appeared in 26 regular-season games with one start, which came at left guard against the New York Jets in 2025. Klein's Buccaneers career page

For a practice-squad addition, that is a decent amount of NFL experience.

Detroit has already brought Mason Miller back after he impressed while handling emergency center duties during the preseason finale. The Lions now add Klein to a practice-squad offensive line that gives them several options if injuries hit the active roster.

That need became more obvious after Cade Mays landed on injured reserve, while Detroit also spent the final weeks of camp sorting through its depth behind a relatively young starting offensive line.

Miller's return gave the Lions one familiar option, and Detroit Sports Nation recently detailed how his unexpected work at center helped earn him another opportunity in the organization. Mason Miller's return to the Lions practice squad

The Lions have also been steadily rebuilding the depth they lost during final roster cuts, with several familiar players returning as Detroit assembled its practice squad Monday. Detroit's first wave of practice-squad additions

Detroit's offensive-line depth was tested during its 25-16 preseason victory over the Indianapolis Colts, and Klein gives the Lions another player capable of covering multiple spots if they need help during the regular season.

He may be starting on the practice squad, but a lineman who can handle four positions and already has 26 NFL games on his résumé is useful insurance to have around.

title: Twins trounce Tigers with homers aplenty
description: The walks sure didn’t help, either.
fullText:
The Tigers went to Minnesota to open a three-game series with their playoff hopes hanging by a thread. They did nothing to assuage their fans' fears on Monday night, dropping said series opener by a 11-1 score.

Starting for the Tigers was Jackson Jobe, making his fifth start this year after recovering from Tommy John surgery. He's struggled with walks: his past two starts have seen him walk three batters in sub-five-inning outings, throwing 86 pitches in each. His stuff has looked good so far, though.

Taj Bradley started for the Twins, and he's been a solid part of their rotation this year; he started his career with a few years in Tampa, and they traded him to Minnesota midway through the 2025 season. His walk rate has really crept up this year to something you shouldn't see in a starter: it was 3.8 per 9 innings coming into today. That wasn't a problem tonight, though.

Minnesota got on the board in the bottom of the first: a leadoff double by Luke Keaschall was followed by a productive groundout and a sacrifice fly by Old Friend™ Kody Clemens. Did you know Clemens had over 20 home runs this year? I sure didn't.

The Twins and Tigers traded nice 5-6-3 double plays in consecutive innings. You don't see that too often.

Clemens wasn't done, though: he mashed a high curveball into the right-field seats for his twenty-third home run of the year to lead off the bottom of the fourth, and the Twins were ahead 2-0. Kevin McGonigle had a rough inning in the field, too: a ground ball slipped under his glove, and on a throw in from the outfield which would've nabbed a runner at second base, he just straight-up dropped it. But a routine fly ball to left field got the Tigers out of the inning without further damage.

Keaschall led off the fifth by reaching base on an error by Hao-Yu Lee at third base, and he stole second. He drew a pickoff attempt by Jobe (heh) which plunked him, so let's just say that the defence wasn't great overall. Clemens walked at the end of a twelve-pitch battle, and Ryan Jeffers followed that with a three-run home run to make it a 5-0 game.

The Tigers got on the board against Bradley with a leadoff no-doubter home run by Lee, going 439 feet into the bullpen to make it a 5-1 game.

Gleyber Torres followed with a sharply-struck single and Colt Keith walked, and you had to wonder, hey, are the Tigers getting something going here? Well, McGonigle flew out to the wall in right field, advancing Torres to third, but alas, Dillon Dingler then hit into a double play and the inning was over. The above clip is, truly, the Tigers' only highlight of the game.

Jobe's night was done after five innings, and his final line was 5 IP, 6 H, 5 R (4 ER), 2 BB, 4 K. So, the control was a little better and the stuff looked decent, but those results just weren't there. The Twins came into tonight's game tied for the most runs scored in the American League, so they aren't exactly pushovers.

Yilber Díaz followed, and while he has a lively arm, he apparently has some trouble controlling where that ball might just end up. He walked the leadoff batter, and after nicely fielding a popup, he walked the next two batters to load the bases with one out. Brooks Lee followed and he cleared said bases with a single; he got thrown out trying to stretch it into a double, but as the old saying goes, "That's like closing the barn door after all the horses have run out."

Meanwhile, Bradley hummed right along into the seventh, and put the maraschino cherry on top of the sundae by striking out Lee on his final pitch of the night; if you round up, it was a 100 mph four-seam fastball and moving all over the place. Tip your cap.

Díaz carried on into the eighth and served up a solo home run to lead off the inning, making it a 9-1 game. But then he got three straight flyouts, so, hooray, I guess?

That extra run allowed Zach McKinstry to take the mound, and John Peck made his Major League debut as a defensive replacement at third base amongst a flurry of defensive changes. McKinstry gave up some runs, of course, but at that point pretty much nobody cared.

Final score: Twins a lot, Tigers not enough

As mentioned, Kody Clemens has over twenty home runs. But did you also know he leads the American League with six triples? I sure didn't know that, either.

It's been a while since Spencer Torkelson's last home run. It was in that Baltimore game near the end of July that we shan't discuss further.

On this day in 1886, an earthquake estimated to be about 7.0 on the Richter scale hit Charleston, South Carolina. If you thought to yourself just now, "I don't think South Carolina is on any major fault lines," you're right: but it's close to a minor fault line in the middle of the North American Plate, and those cracks can definitely produce earthquakes.

fullText:
The US Open began on Sunday - and there is comprehensive coverage of the final Grand Slam of the year across the BBC.

The world's top players will gather in New York where, in addition to one of the sport's major prizes, record prize money is on line.

From the return of entertainer Carlos Alcaraz in the men's singles to an eagerly anticipated doubles reunion for Serena and Venus Williams, here is all you need to know.

The US Open main draw begins on Sunday, 30 August.

The 15-day hard court tournament concludes with the men's singles final on Sunday, 13 September, with the women's a day before.

The mixed doubles competition, which became a standalone two-day competition in 2025, took place earlier in the week.

Czech pair Jakub Mensik and Karolina Muchova walked away with the title and $1m in prize money.

Muchova & Mensik win US Open mixed doubles title

Alcaraz and Williams thrill in US Open mixed doubles

Spain's Alcaraz defeated Italian rival Jannik Sinner 6-2 3-6 6-1 6-4 to win the US Open men's singles title last year.

The women's singles title was won by Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka, who beat American Amanda Anisimova 6-3 7-6 (7-3).

The men's doubles competition was won by Spain's Marcel Granollers and Argentine Horacio Zeballos, while Canada's Gabriela Dabrowski and New Zealand's Erin Routliffe won the women's event.

Japan's Tokito Oda and Yui Kamiji won the men's and women's wheelchair singles titles respectively, while Dutchman Niels Vink took the men's quad wheelchair title.

The BBC Sport website will bring you live text commentaries, reports, features and analysis across the fortnight.

BBC Radio 5 Live Sport will provide daily commentaries live from the Arthur Ashe Stadium in New York across BBC Sounds.

Tennis correspondent Russell Fuller will be joined by fellow commentators Katie Smith, Abigail Johnson and David Law, plus summarisers Annabel Croft, Pat Cash, Daniela Hantuchova, Mark Woodforde and Leon Smith.

There will also be podcasts recapping the biggest stories from of the tournament - just search 'tennis' on BBC Sounds to find it.

Two of Britain's big hopes in the singles competitions - Emma Raducanu and Jack Draper - have announced they will not compete at the US Open.

Former US Open winner Raducanu is continuing her recovery from a stress fracture.

The 23-year-old sustained the injury during the grass-court season and was forced to make a late decision to pull out of Wimbledon.

Meanwhile, Draper, a semi-finalist in 2024, has withdrawn because of the long-term arm injury that has stalled his progress.

The 24-year-old former British number one was ranked inside the world's top five when he suffered bone bruising in his left serving arm and has played just 16 matches in the past 12 months.

British qualifier Toby Samuel registered his first win at a Grand Slam with a commanding victory over Tomas Machac on the opening day's play.

Jacob Fearnley, who reached the main draw as a lucky loser, produced a battling five-set victory to reach the second round.

However, British number one Cameron Norrie lost in four sets to Luca Van Assche.

British number one Katie Boulter also reached the first round with a battling 6-4 3-6 6-0 win over American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee.

Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery, Jan Choinski, and qualifier Harry Wendelken all play later in the week.

Harriet Dart and Francesca Jones also won all three of their qualifying matches, marking the first time four British players have progressed to the main draws of an overseas Grand Slam since the 1988 Australian Open.

Dart reached the second round with a comeback win over American Peyton Stearns.

Samuel breaks more new ground with first win at a Slam

The wait for the return of the exciting rivalry between Alcaraz and Sinner goes on.

Sinner and Alcaraz produced a clean sweep of the Grand Slam titles in both 2024 and 2025, winning four majors apiece in a duopoly which has morphed into a generational duel.

But the pair have not played at the same Grand Slam since January's Australian Open.

Alcaraz was forced to miss the French Open and Wimbledon because of a wrist problem, while a knee issue has ruled Sinner out of the US Open.

Sinner has not competed since he lifted his fifth career Grand Slam singles title by beating Alexander Zverev at the All England Club in July.

Alcaraz, meanwhile, made his return to competitive action alongside American great Serena in the mixed doubles competition in New York on Tuesday, reaching the quarter-finals.

Novak Djokovic was bidding for a standalone record 25th Grand Slam title but suffered a gruelling first-round exit to Mariano Navone.

'I felt the love' - how did Alcaraz look on winning singles return?

Djokovic's tearful loss leaves future uncertain

In the women's event, world number one Sabalenka is aiming to become the first woman since Serena Williams in 2014 to win the title three years in a row.

However, Sabalenka is in shaky form, with her top ranking also under threat.

Elena Rybakina - who beat Sabalenka to win the Australian Open in January - will become number one if she reaches the semi-finals regardless of other results.

Rybakina can become number one without playing a match provided Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff do not win the title.

One of the big occasions at this year's tournament will be the return of the Williams sisters in a Grand Slam doubles competition.

Serena and Venus have been given a wildcard for the women's doubles, and 46-year-old Venus will also play singles in New York.

Williams sisters given US Open doubles wildcard

The draws for the men's and women's singles competitions at the US Open took place on Thursday, 27 August.

Alcaraz faces Russia's Roman Safiullin in the first round while Sabalenka will play Colombia's Camila Osorio.

Who plays who in the US Open first round?

The top seeds in the men's draw are:

The top seeds in the women's draw are:

The US Open is this year offering the biggest prize fund in Grand Slam history with a total of $108m (£79.2m) up for grabs - marking a 20% increase on last year.

The singles' champions will receive $5.5m (£4.03m) each in a 10% increase on 2025.

First-round losers will take home $140,000 (£102,667) - which is $30,000 and 27% more than last year.

The prize pool includes a $2m (£1.47m) contribution to a welfare fund, which leading players have been demanding from all the Grand Slams.

US Open offers biggest prize fund in Grand Slam history

The mixed doubles took place from 24-26 August.

Muchova and Mensik paired up for the first time to win the mixed doubles title, beating Flavio Cobolli and Belinda Bencic in the final.

The tournament's revamped mixed doubles format has attracted criticism for favouring the allure of the sport's top singles stars at the expense of established doubles players.

But the crowds turned out and produced a terrific atmosphere for the tournament's headline act, Alcaraz and Williams, with about 15,000 people watching inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The women's doubles begins on Thursday, 3 September, and the men's event gets under way on Friday, 4 September.

30 August-1 September: Men's and women's singles first round

2-3 September: Men's and women's singles second round

3 September: Men's doubles begins

4-5 September: Men's and women's singles third round

4 September: Women's doubles begins

6-7 September: Men's and women's singles fourth round

8 September: Wheelchair doubles begins

8-9 September: Men's and women's singles quarter-finals

9 September: Wheelchair singles begins

10 September: Women's singles semi-finals

11 September: Men's singles semi-finals, wheelchair doubles finals

12 September: Women's singles final, men's doubles final, wheelchair singles finals

13 September: Men's singles final

title: Tigers crushed again in loss as Twins put on power show
description: Detroit Tigers score: Jackson Jobe allowed five runs (four earned) in five innings as his teammates struggled against Taj Bradley on Monday.
fullText:
MINNEAPOLIS – It was like watching water circle the drain.

Everything in a spiral. Flowing toward a narrow opening. Gravity tugging it all down. The result all but inevitable.

The Detroit Tigers played sloppy defense against the Minnesota Twins on Monday, Aug. 31. They didn't generate much offense. Jackson Jobe gave up four earned runs, including a pair of homers, en route to five overall. The bullpen gave up four more until Zach McKinstry was brought in to end the misery, though he gave up two more. And the result was all but inevitable – gurgle, gurgle, gurgle – as the Minnesota Twins spanked the Tigers, 11-1, at Target Field.

Which is the fitting theme for what the Tigers have experienced over more than two weeks.

The Tigers (63-74) have now lost 13 of 16 games, dating to August 14.

What has been the big problem? The offense has disappeared.

Consider this: The Tigers began August with a fine 8-3 record and had a plus-40 run differential in just that month.

But in their past 16 games? They have won just three times while being outscored by 35 runs.

Monday's loss dropped the Tigers to six games back in the American League wild-card chase, with the Cleveland Guardians idle, and 9½ back in the AL Central with 25 games to play.

The Tigers are in a weird position. They are still talking about fighting to make the playoffs, even if the odds are against them (and get decidedly worse every day). But they are also in the midst of a youth movement, stacking the roster with rookies. On Monday, they brought up shortstop John Peck, a 2023 draft pick who made his MLB debut in the eighth inning and is expected to start on Tuesday.

"We've watched young players come up and contribute, and so the message doesn't really change – the expectation doesn't change," Tigers manager A.J. Hinch said before the game. "We are where we are, and we know we have to be really, really good to make this a memorable September."

Well, the final day of August was anything but memorable.

Because they couldn't get anything going against Twins starter Taj Bradley, who was simply brilliant. He threw seven dominant innings, allowing just one run while recording nine strikeouts.

Bradley was coming off an 11-strikeout performance against the Athletics on Aug. 25, including the first immaculate inning in Twins history. He wasn't immaculate against the Tigers, but he was a dominant force.

Bradley allowed only one hit through the first four innings – a Hao-Yu Lee single to right. Then again, this looked awfully familiar. Bradley dominated the Tigers on April 7 in a 6⅓-inning performance, allowing just one run and striking out 10.

The one bright spot for the Tigers?

Lee crushed a homer to center that had an exit velocity of 109.6 mph and traveled 439 feet.

The Twins came into this game with a certain style.

"This is a team across the way that's pretty aggressive," Hinch said before the game. "You rarely get to four-pitch at-bats. These guys want to swing the bat."

And that's what they did against Jobe.

Luke Keaschall doubled on Jobe's second pitch Monday. After he moved to third on a fielder's choice, former Tiger Kody Clemens hit a sacrifice fly to give the Twins a 1-0 lead.

Clemens caused more damage in the fourth inning when he crushed a hanging curve that was actually out of the strike zone.

Jobe was in deep trouble in the fourth after a walk, hit and error. But he got out of it with a pair of harmless popups.

Keaschall was a pain in the fifth inning as well. After he got on by a Lee error, Keaschall stole second base – off Jobe. Keaschall seemed to mess with Jobe, taking a massive lead off second; it seemed to mess up the young righty as Jobe walked Clemens to create another tenuous moment. Then Twins catcher Ryan Jeffers hit a three-run homer, his 11th of the season.

Troy Melton (7-3, 1.86) will take the mound for the Tigers when they face the Twins in the second game of this three-game series on Tuesday (7:40 p.m., Detroit SportsNet). Lefty Connor Prielipp (3-7, 5.55) will start for Minnesota.

Contact Jeff Seidel: jseidel@freepress.com. Follow him on X @seideljeff

title: Michigan State offensive lineman nominated for 2026 Campbell Trophy
description: A Michigan State offensive lineman was nominated for the 2026 Campbell Trophy.
fullText:
Michigan State football brought in North Dakota State center transfer Trent Fraley in to patrol the middle of their offensive line in 2026. Not only will Fraley be a big help on the field, but by all accounts, Fraley is a top leader and a great person to have off of the field.

Fraley's off field presence was made known even more when he was named as Michigan State's nominee for the Campbell Trophy. Awarded by the National Football Federation, the Campbell Trophy is given to a player with the best combination of academics, leadership and on-field performance. It has been dubbed as the "Academic Heisman."

Michigan State has never had a winner of the Campbell Trophy, meaning Fraley has a chance to make program history this season if he were to win the award.
